## REQUIRED STRUCTURE OF YOUR AUDIT REPORT

Please format your response into the following four clear sections:
1. **Executive Forensic Audit Summary:** Concise synthesis of the group's true economic performance, balance sheet health, post-balance-sheet liquidity runway, and key findings.
2. **Detailed Forensic Reasoning & Determinations:** Step-by-step walkthrough of each key retail junction (weighted-average basic & diluted share count and continuing HEPS reconciliation, merchandise vs credit/other revenue, gross profit margin bridge, debtors book health & IFRS 9 ECL provisioning, store network capex and trading density, IFRS 16 lease liability structure, post-year-end trading, and cash conversion / dividend payout), citing specific notes, tables, and calculations.
3. **Audit of Common Surface-Reading Pitfalls:** Contrast your findings against the common errors made by naive readers.
4. **Final Forensic Verification Matrix:** A clean markdown summary table listing each Junction, the Raw Initial Claim, the Resolving Note/SENS Announcement, and your Final Verified Determination.

## MANDATORY ACCOUNTING & VALUATION GUARDRAILS REGISTRY (SECTOR: RETAIL)

The following institutional guardrails are enforced from the SQLite `sector_guardrails` registry based on prior forensic audits. Violating any of these rules invalidates the report:

| Rule Code | Scope | Guardrail Title | Mandatory Enforcement Rule |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| `ALL-IFRS16-EV-BRIDGE` | **UNIVERSAL** | **IFRS 16 EV-to-Equity & Cash Flow Consistency** *(Origin: SPP)* | Never mix Pre-IFRS 16 cash flows/EBITDA with Post-IFRS 16 lease debt in an Enterprise Value (EV) to Equity bridge. If EV is derived by discounting or applying a multiple to Pre-IFRS 16 EBITDA/FCFF (where cash lease rental payments are already deducted as an operating outflow), DO NOT subtract capitalised IFRS 16 lease liabilities again in the EV-to-Equity bridge (and do not subtract lease principal payments a second time in FCFE). Conversely, if subtracting net IFRS 16 lease liabilities in the EV bridge, you must discount Post-IFRS 16 EBITDA/FCFF before lease payments. Always state explicitly whether your valuation bridge is on a Pre-IFRS 16 or Post-IFRS 16 basis. |
| `ALL-PNL-VERTICAL-ARITHMETIC` | **UNIVERSAL** | **Statutory vs. Normalized P&L Vertical Arithmetic & Impairment Bridge** *(Origin: SPP)* | Every income statement table must sum vertically line-by-line (Revenue - Cost of sales = Gross profit; Gross profit + Other revenue/income - Net operating expenses = Operating profit). Always verify from the primary AFS notes whether statutory Operating Profit is already stated AFTER impairments, restructuring, or extraordinary items before subtracting them; never subtract Note 7/exceptional impairments a second time from a statutory Operating Profit that already includes them, and ensure historical continuing PAT and HEPS match the statutory AFS reconciliation identically. |
| `ALL-SHARE-COUNT-ANCHOR` | **UNIVERSAL** | **Verified Weighted-Average Share Count & Continuing HEPS Denominator** *(Origin: SPP)* | Always extract and state the exact basic and diluted weighted-average number of ordinary shares (in millions, net of treasury shares) from the AFS EPS/HEPS note. Never confuse Headline Earnings in R'm with the share count in millions. In Stage 2 Section 3, include an explicit 'Weighted-Average Shares (m)' row immediately above 'Continuing HEPS (cents)', divide Continuing Headline Earnings (excluding discontinued operations and capital/Note 7 items) by that exact share count, and verify that full-year forecast HEPS is consistent with H1 continuing HEPS already banked. |
| `ALL-TREASURY-SHARE-DIVIDEND-BRIDGE` | **UNIVERSAL** | **Gross vs. Net Treasury Share Count & Parent vs. Consolidated Dividend Reconciliation** *(Origin: CGR)* | Before flagging an arithmetic discrepancy between parent-company dividends paid/declared and net shares in issue, always check gross issued shares vs treasury shares held by subsidiaries or share trusts (e.g. in the Integrated Report dividend declaration or Stated Capital note). Under South African corporate law, the parent company pays the gross dividend on all gross issued shares, whereas the Consolidated Statement of Changes in Equity and Cash Flow Statement eliminate intra-group dividends paid on treasury shares. |
| `ALL-ENTITY-ACRONYM-DISAMBIGUATION` | **UNIVERSAL** | **Full Legal Entity Name Verification Across Notes (No Acronym Conflation)** *(Origin: CGR)* | Never abbreviate two distinct legal entities to the same acronym and claim an accounting classification contradiction. When evaluating entities with similar names, acronyms, or operating divisions, always compare and cross-check full legal entity names across notes before concluding on whether an entity is a joint venture, joint operation, associate, or subsidiary. |
| `ALL-DCF-REPRODUCIBILITY` | **UNIVERSAL** | **DCF Schedule Reproducibility & Anti-Handwaving Component Bridge** *(Origin: DCP)* | Mandates explicit disclosure of annual forecast FCFF/FCFE, terminal value, WACC/discount rate, and a step-by-step numerical EV-to-Equity bridge. Forbids applying qualitative, unmodeled percentage uplifts to blended valuation components; any adjustment between underlying component valuations (e.g. DCF and P/E) and the published target price must be modeled directly within the underlying cash flows or valuation multiples. |
| `ALL-CASHFLOW-CLASSIFICATION-BRIDGE` | **UNIVERSAL** | **Statutory Operating Cash Flow to FCFF/FCFE Bridge & Capex/Lease Deduction** *(Origin: DCP)* | Prohibits labeling statutory Cash Generated from Operations (before capex, lease principal repayments, and interest) as Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE) or Free Cash Flow to Firm (FCFF). Models must explicitly bridge operating cash flow to true free cash flow by deducting replacement and expansion capex, IFRS 16 lease principal repayments, net finance costs, and working capital normalizations. |
| `ALL-CASH-ROLLFORWARD-CONSISTENCY` | **UNIVERSAL** | **Forecast Cash and Financing Must Reconcile** *(Origin: NTU)* | For every forecast period, reconcile opening cash plus operating, investing and financing cash flows and separately identified FX or scope changes to closing cash on the forecast balance sheet. Reconcile new borrowing, repayments and equity issuance to debt balances, equity and dilution. State the cash definition and rounding tolerance; bridge restricted cash, held-for-sale cash and overdrafts included in cash equivalents explicitly, without double counting. An unresolved material residual invalidates the forecast and dependent valuation; missing inputs are NOT VERIFIED, never PASS. Example: opening 100 + operating 20 - capex 10 + financing 5 = closing 115 passes; opening 100 plus net change -815 cannot produce closing 95 without an explicit 810 reconciling inflow. |
| `ALL-SENSITIVITY-REPRODUCIBILITY` | **UNIVERSAL** | **Sensitivity Cells Must Reproduce the Valuation** *(Origin: NTU)* | Recalculate every sensitivity cell using the same documented base valuation formula, changing only the named inputs. The central case MUST reproduce the published base target within a declared rounding tolerance. Preserve debt, share count, cash-flow basis, valuation bridges and all discounts unless explicitly varied. Show the formula and full transformation for any additional haircut; unexplained cells invalidate the sensitivity conclusions. Nonlinear models are allowed when their actual formulas are used; do not impose constant derivatives from another method. Missing formulas or inputs are NOT VERIFIED. Example: with 3,845 million of PBD assets, a 0.05 multiple change and one 25% discount over 780.7 million shares imply a 0.18469 ZAR/share change; 0.07 without a disclosed transformation fails. This supplements SOTP arithmetic and prohibits double counting adjustments. |
| `ALL-EQUITY-NAV-VS-CONTRIBUTED-CAPITAL` | **UNIVERSAL** | **Ordinary Shareholder NAV versus Contributed Capital** *(Origin: NTU)* | Calculate statutory ordinary book value/NAV per share from equity attributable to parent ordinary shareholders, excluding non-controlling interests and preference or other non-ordinary claims, divided by ordinary shares outstanding net of treasury shares at the same measurement date. Reconcile retained earnings or accumulated losses and reserves; never label contributed share capital alone as NAV. Use date-matched closing shares rather than silently substituting an earnings weighted-average denominator. Adjusted or tangible NAV is permitted only when clearly labelled and reconciled to statutory ordinary equity, with every adjustment disclosed. NAV is not automatically market fair value. Example: parent ordinary equity 1,329 million / 780.651033 million net shares = approximately 1.70 ZAR/share; share capital 5,410 million / those shares is not book NAV. |
| `ALL-MATERIAL-ISSUES-VALUATION-WITHHOLD` | **UNIVERSAL** | **Withhold Valuation Until Material Dependencies Are Resolved** *(Origin: NTU)* | If a material cash-flow, forecast, financing, share-count, portfolio or valuation dependency fails reconciliation or remains unsupported, return VALUATION WITHHELD - MATERIAL ISSUES UNRESOLVED. Preserve verified historical analysis and risks, identify each blocker and the evidence or correction needed, and carry unresolved Stage 1 findings forward. Do not publish a target, rating bands, upside, dividend yield, TSR or investment recommendation; use JSON null, never zero or HOLD. Illustrative scenarios must remain clearly conditional and separate from the headline valuation. READY requires explicit source evidence, consistent periods and scopes, cash/debt/portfolio roll-forwards, equity financing and terminal-policy consistency, valuation-bridge and sensitivity checks. Assumptions may be used when supported and disclosed; they cannot conceal material missing inputs. Application checks of declared evidence and numeric reconciliations do not replace independent review. |
| `RETAIL-IFRS16-HEADLEASE-SUBLEASE` | **RETAIL** | **Retail Head-Lease Liability vs. Back-to-Back Franchisee Lease Receivable Netting** *(Origin: SPP)* | For wholesale/franchise retailers that sign head-leases on properties and sub-lease them back-to-back to independent retailers, always net the IFRS 16 finance lease receivables (Current + Non-current) against gross IFRS 16 lease liabilities to isolate the group's true net store/DC lease exposure, and distinguish Pre-IFRS 16 covenant EBITDA from Post-IFRS 16 statutory EBITDA. |
| `RETAIL-ECL-CASHFLOW-VS-ALLOWANCE` | **RETAIL** | **Retail & Trade Receivable ECL Non-Cash Movement vs. Balance Sheet Allowance Bridge** *(Origin: SPP)* | When auditing trade/retailer receivables and loan allowances, reconcile the Cash Flow Statement non-cash ECL movement against the Balance Sheet allowance movement by accounting for final write-offs against the allowance and fair-value discounting, and verify whether elevated credit loss run-rates persist in post-balance-sheet SENS updates. |
| `RETAIL-APM-OPERATING-MARGIN` | **RETAIL** | **Retail APM Merchandise Margin vs. Total Statutory Operating Margin** *(Origin: LEW)* | The model must strictly distinguish non-standard Alternative Performance Measures (APMs) that calculate operating margins by dividing group EBIT solely by merchandise sales from true statutory operating margins on total revenue (including credit finance and insurance income). Models must disclose both and base consolidated operational forecasts on statutory total revenue. |
| `RETAIL-HIDDEN-ARREARS-AUDIT` | **RETAIL** | **Retail Customer Credit Hidden Arrears inside Satisfactory Paid Accounts** *(Origin: LEW)* | When auditing credit-granting retailers, the model must not rely on reported 'Satisfactory Paid' percentage claims without probing whether overdue instalments are concealed within performing categories. The true contractual delinquency and non-performing debt ratio must be explicitly quantified in working capital and impairment assumptions. |
| `RETAIL-WORKING-CAPITAL-PAYABLE-STRETCH` | **RETAIL** | **Working Capital Payable Stretch & Cash Conversion Normalization** *(Origin: DCP)* | Forbids treating operating cash flow spikes as sustainable free cash flow when driven predominantly by elongation of trade creditor days (>15% YoY increase in trade payables) or inventory freezes during network store expansion. Analysts must normalize working capital swings to multi-year historical averages and isolate supplier rebate/allowance reclassifications from core merchandise gross margins. |

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Non-audit services qualification** [D001, p. 8]: "Non-audit services provided by the external auditors (Forvis Mazars) in the current financial year amounted to **R230,000 (2025: R238,400)**. These fees related to agreed-upon procedures for turnover certificates." — This is a small, declining non-audit fee (down ~3.5% YoY), consistent with auditor independence. No forecast impact beyond confirming no large consulting leakage; verify total audit fee in D005 notes to compute non-audit/audit ratio.
- **Auditor tenure qualification** [D001, p. 7]: "The external auditors and the audit partner, Danielle Keeve, have been the auditors of the Group for **five years**. The rotation of the partner will occur at least every five years." — Partner rotation is imminent; a rotation does not change reported numbers but may change KAM emphasis/estimates in FY2027. Flag for D005/D006.
- **Materiality basis** [D001, p. 9]: 8% of profit before tax → consolidated materiality R111,572,000 implies **implied consolidated PBT ≈ R1,394,650,000** (111,572,000 ÷ 0.08). Separate materiality R54,747,000 implies **implied company PBT ≈ R684,337,500**. These are derived benchmarks, not reported PBT — must be reconciled to the actual statement of comprehensive income in D002. This is a key arithmetic cross-check.
- **Going-concern qualification** [D001, p. 7]: Committee "reviews the basis on which the company has been determined a going concern and makes a recommendation to the Board." — Confirms a going-concern assessment was performed but gives no headroom/covenant figures; must be tested against cash flow statement (D002) and going-concern note (D005).

        Group Audit Scope                                                         
        We tailored the scope of our audit to perform sufficient work to enable us to provide an opinion on the consolidated financial statements
        as a whole, considering the structure of the group, the accounting processes and controls and the industry in which the group operates.
        We performed risk assessment procedures to determine which of the group’s components are likely to include risks of material
        misstatement to the consolidated financial statements, and identified which further audit procedures are required to be performed at
        component level to address those risks.                                   
        We identified 66 components of which 40 were subjected to full scope audits conducted by the group engagement team. We identified
        7 components where audit procedures were performed on one or more classes of transactions, account balances or disclosures based
        on the assessed risks of material misstatement at group level. Based on our risk assessment procedures, we have determined that
        there is a less than reasonable possibility of a material misstatement in the remaining financial information not subject to further audit
        procedures. The remaining 19 components were classified as out of scope components.
        The group engagement team through the full scope audits of the 40 components and the audit work on one or more classes of
        transactions, accounted balances or disclosures of the 7 components audited:
        • 99% of Revenue,                                                         
        • 96% of Profit Before Tax, and                                           
        • 99% of Total Assets.                                                    
        We sent detailed audit instructions to the 7 in scope component auditors where audit procedures were performed on one or more
        classes of transaction, account balances or disclosures, covering the significant areas and the information required to be reported to
        us. Based on our risk assessment, we determined the level of involvement in component audits. We reviewed key working papers and
        conclusions. We communicated regularly with the component auditors during various stages of the audit.
        Key Audit Matters                                                         
        Key audit matters are those matters that, in our professional judgement, were of most significance in our audit of the consolidated and
        separate financial statements of the current period. These matters were addressed in the context of our audit of the consolidated and
        separate financial statements as a whole, and in forming our opinion thereon and we do not provide a separate opinion on these matters.
        In terms of the EAR Rule, we are required to report the outcome of audit procedures or key observations with respect to the key audit
        matters and these are included below.                                     
        Rebates and advertising agreements (accounting policy note 3.6 and disclosure notes 8 and 16)
        Description of As described in Significant accounting estimates, judgements, and assumptions – Advertising agreements in
        the key audit accounting policy note 3.6, and as disclosed in notes 8 and 16, the group and company recognise a reduction in
        matter    the cost of inventories sold and held at year end or include as other income amounts from suppliers with regards to
                  rebate and advertising agreements.                              
                  The calculations of the rebate and advertising agreements’ accounting adjustments are, with exception of
                  conditional contracts, not automated and are managed centrally. Due to the large volume and variety of rebate
                  and advertising agreements, we considered that the completeness, occurrence and accuracy of the rebate and
                  advertising agreements and their resulting accounting adjustments required significant audit attention.
                  The rebate agreements primarily comprise of contributions received in relation to:
                  • Retail business promotions                                    
                  • Annual volume-based rebates                                   
                  • Wholesale logistic rebates                                    
                  • Other general rebates.

                   differences on the recording of rebate and advertising agreements accounting adjustments in the general ledger.
                  Evaluated the accuracy and occurrence of the rebate and advertising agreements accounting adjustments by
                  performing the following procedures on manually calculated transactions:
                  • Traced a sample of transactions through to signed supplier agreements, related invoices, and proof of settlement
                   to establish the occurrence of the transactions.               
                  • Re-performed the calculations obtained from management with reference to the underlying data, and the
                   contractual performance obligations to assess the accuracy of the transactions.
                  We further confirmed with reference to the agreements whether the rebate and advertising agreements accounting
                  adjustments were accounted for accurately and completely in the current financial period.
                  In relation to the automated conditional contracts:             
                  • A sample of conditional contracts was selected to corroborate that the contract term’s manual inputs for
                   automation are valid and that the terms uploaded into the system are accurate.
                  Assessed the reasonability of the accounting adjustment related to rebates on the valuation of unsold inventory at
                  year end.                                                       
                  Assessed the reasonability of the rebate and advertising agreement accounting adjustments as either other income
                  in terms of IFRS 15 Revenue or as a reduction in cost of inventories sold and held at year end in terms of the
                  requirements of IAS 2 Inventories.                              
                  Based on the procedures performed as detailed above, we did not raise any material exceptions with respect to our
                  audit of completeness, occurrence and accuracy of rebates and advertising agreements.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) with definitions appear in this capture.** The only cross-references are to *accounting policy note 3.6* and *disclosure notes 8 and 16* (rebates/advertising). **The text of note 3.6, note 8 and note 16 is NOT in this capture** — must be verified in D005/D006. Do not assume their content.
- **KAM "Rebates and advertising agreements" — forecast implications** `[D001, physical PDF pp. 10–11]`:
  - The adjustment is split between **reduction of cost of inventories sold and held at year end (IAS 2)** and **other income (IFRS 15)**. This means reported **gross margin and "other income" are both partly supplier-funded**, not pure merchandise economics. For forecasting, the split between the two treatments must be extracted from notes 8 and 16 — otherwise gross margin % and other-income line will be mis-modelled.
  - Auditor notes calculations are **"not automated and managed centrally"** except conditional contracts — a manual-estimate risk. Any change in supplier agreement terms or volume thresholds directly moves gross margin. Flag as a margin-bridge sensitivity.
  - Auditor conclusion: **no material exceptions** — supports reliability of the rebate adjustment as a forecast base, but the *quantum* is still unverified here.
- **Group audit scope qualification** `[D001, physical PDF p. 10]`: 19 of 66 components "out of scope" with "less than reasonable possibility of material misstatement." Coverage of 99% revenue / 96% PBT / 99% total assets implies **~4% of PBT sits outside tested components** — a residual estimation risk for the profit forecast, though small.
- **"Other information" clean statement** `[D001, physical PDF p. 11]`: no inconsistency flagged between audited statements and the directors'/committee reports — mildly supportive that narrative guidance elsewhere is not contradicted by the audit.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note cross-references on equity statement** `[D002, physical PDF p. 15]`: Share capital → Note 19; Treasury shares → Note 20; Dividends → Note 21. These are the only footnote markers; **no footnote definition text is present in this capture** — the actual Note 19/20/21 content is missing and must be verified in D005/D006. Do not infer treasury-share or dividend detail beyond the reserve movements shown.
- **"Other reserves" column is blank in the Group table** `[D002, physical PDF p. 15]`: The Group statement shows a column headed "Other reserves" with no values, while the Company statement shows an "Other reserves" column with balances (opening (R3,917,019k) → closing (R3,908,665k)) `[D002, physical PDF p. 16]`. This is a presentation inconsistency — the Group "Other reserves" balance (which should reconcile to the (R4,566,716k) "reserves" figure) is not separately disclosed. Verification needed.
- **"Change in ownership interest in subsidiary and acquisitions" R10,746k (FY2025) vs "Change in ownership interest in subsidiary" (R22,011k) (FY2026)** `[D002, physical PDF p. 15]`: FY2026 shows a **negative** R22,011k equity movement with NCI +R12,384k and retained earnings (R34,395k). This is a cash outflow in financing (R22,011k) `[D002, physical PDF p. 17]` — consistent with an NCI buy-out. Nature (which subsidiary, price vs book) not disclosed here; verify in Note 5/27.4.
- **"Common control adjustment" (R2,654k) appears only in Company FY2025** `[D002, physical PDF p. 16]`: No FY2026 equivalent. Confirm no common-control transaction in FY2026.
- **Cash flow — "Cash inflow from trading operations" R3,124,134k is NOT operating cash flow** `[D002, physical PDF p. 17]`: It is a pre-working-capital, pre-finance/tax/dividend subtotal. True OCF (before dividends, which are classified here within operating activities) = 3,124,134 + 125,820 + 28,492 − 559,644 − 401,870 = **R2,316,932k**; after dividends paid R524,221k = R1,792,711k (the stated "Cash flow from operating activities" line). Note dividends are classified **within operating activities**, which is a presentation choice affecting FCF comparability — verify against accounting policy (Note 3) in D005.
- **"Cash and cash equivalents at end of year" is negative R1,166,964k** `[D002, physical PDF p. 17]`: This equals the net overdraft (cash R499,756k less bank overdraft R1,666,720k per prior capture). A negative "cash and cash equivalents" balance implies the overdraft is presented net within cash equivalents — verify Note 27.5 and whether the overdraft is a revolving facility subject to covenant/going-concern disclosure.
- **Finance costs paid R559,644k vs finance income received R28,492k** `[D002, physical PDF p. 17]`: Net finance cost cash R531,152k. This includes lease finance charges (IFRS 16) — split between interest on loans and lease interest not shown here; verify Note 22/23.
- **JV acquisition R189,000k (2025: R155,940k) and business combination R23,475k (2025: nil)** `[D002, physical PDF p. 17]`: Recurring JV investment (two consecutive years) — capital allocation pattern to note; business combination is new in FY2026. Verify Note 4/5 for identity and returns.
- **Company "Increase in investments" R254,534k (2025: R172,540k)** `[D002, physical PDF p. 17]`: Company-level investment into subsidiaries/JVs; reconcile to Group Note 15.

        1. Corporate information                                                  
                                                                                  
           Dis-Chem Pharmacies Limited is incorporated in South Africa. The Group annual financial statements as at 28 February 2026
           comprise the company and its subsidiaries (collectively referred to as “the Group”).
        2. Basis of preparation                                                   
                                                                                  
           The Group and company annual financial statements set out on pages 2 to 82 are prepared on the historical cost basis as
           modified by fair value adjustments, and incorporate the following principal accounting policies, which conform with IFRS
           Accounting Standards as issued by the IASB, its IFRIC interpretations and SA Financial Reporting Requirements, the JSE
           Listings Requirements and the Companies Act of South Africa.           
           The Group and company annual financial statements are presented in South African Rands and are rounded to the nearest
           thousand, except where otherwise indicated. The financial statements are prepared on the going concern basis.
        3. Summary of material accounting policies                                
           The material accounting policies applied in the preparation of the annual financial statements are set out in the relevant
           supporting notes, unless no supporting note is presented or it impacts multiple line items. In the latter case they are presented
           under 3.1 to 3.6 below. These policies have been consistently applied to all the years presented, unless otherwise stated in
           note 3.7.                                                              
           3.1 Basis of consolidation                                             
              The Group annual consolidated financial statements comprise the financial statements of the Group and its subsidiaries
              as at 28�February.                                                  
              Generally, there is a presumption that a majority of voting rights results in control. To support this presumption and
              when the Group has less than a majority of the voting or similar rights of an investee, the Group considers all relevant
              facts and circumstances in assessing whether it has power over an investee, including:
              • the contractual arrangement with the other vote holders of the investee; and
              • the Group’s voting rights and potential voting rights.            
              Consolidation of a subsidiary begins when the Group obtains control over the subsidiary and ceases when the Group
              loses control of the subsidiary. Assets, liabilities, income and expenses of a subsidiary acquired or disposed of during the
              year are included in the consolidated annual financial statements from the date the Group gains control until the date
              the Group ceases to control the subsidiary.                         
              Profit or loss and each component of other comprehensive income (OCI) are attributed to the equity holders of the
              parent of the Group and to the non-controlling interests, even if this results in the non-controlling interests having a
              deficit balance. When necessary, adjustments are made to the financial statements of subsidiaries to bring their
              accounting policies in line with the Group’s accounting policies. All intra-Group assets and liabilities, equity, income,
              expenses and cash flows relating to transactions between members of the Group are eliminated in full on consolidation.
              A change in the ownership interest of a subsidiary, without a loss of control, is accounted for as an equity transaction.
           3.2 Business combinations and goodwill                                 
                                                                                  
              Business combinations, other than those under common control, are accounted for using the acquisition method. The
              cost of an acquisition is measured as the aggregate of the consideration transferred measured at acquisition date fair
              value and the amount of any non-controlling interests in the acquiree. For each business combination, the Group
              measures the non-controlling interests in the acquiree at the proportionate share of the acquiree’s identifiable net assets.
              Acquisition-related costs are expensed as incurred and included in other expenses.
              When the Group/company acquires a business, it assesses the financial assets and liabilities assumed for appropriate
              classification and designation in accordance with the contractual terms, economic circumstances and pertinent
              conditions as at the acquisition date.                              
              Any contingent consideration to be transferred by the acquirer is recognised at fair value at the acquisition date.
              Contingent consideration classified as an asset or liability that is a financial instrument is measured at fair value with
              changes in fair value recognised in profit or loss.

        NOTES      TO   THE   GROUP      AND     COMPANY                          
                                                                                  
        ANNUAL       FINANCIAL        STATEMENTS                                  
                                                                                  
        for the year ended 28 February 2026                                       
                                                                                  
              Goodwill is initially measured at cost, being the excess of the aggregate of the consideration transferred and the amount
              recognised for non-controlling interests, and any previous interest held, over the fair value of the net identifiable assets
              acquired and liabilities assumed.                                   
              After initial recognition, goodwill is measured at cost less any accumulated impairment losses. For the purpose of
              impairment testing, goodwill acquired in a business combination is, from the acquisition date, allocated to each of the
              Group’s/company's cash-generating units (CGUs) that are expected to benefit from the combination, irrespective of
              whether other assets or liabilities of the acquiree are assigned to those units.
           3.3 Impairment of non-financial assets                                 
                                                                                  
              At each reporting date, the carrying amounts of tangible and intangible assets are reviewed to determine whether there
              is any indication that those assets may be impaired. If any such indication exists, the recoverable amount of the asset is
              estimated in order to determine the extent of the impairment loss (if any). Where it is not possible to estimate the
              recoverable amount for an individual asset, the recoverable amount is determined for the CGU to which the asset
              belongs. Where a reasonable and consistent basis of allocation can be identified, corporate assets are also allocated to
              individual CGUs, or otherwise they are allocated to the smallest group of CGUs for which a reasonable and consistent
              allocation basis can be identified.                                 
              The recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value-in-use. In assessing value-in-use, the
              estimated future cash flows per the management accounts for the next five years are discounted to their present value
              using a pre-tax discount rate that reflects current market assessments of the time value of money and the risks specific to
              the asset. In determining fair value less costs of disposal, recent market transactions are taken into account. If no such
              transactions can be identified, an appropriate valuation model is used.
              If the recoverable amount of an asset (or CGU) is estimated to be less than its carrying amount, the carrying amount of
              the asset (or CGU) is reduced to its recoverable amount. Impairment losses are recognised as an expense immediately in
              profit or loss.                                                     
              For goodwill and intangible assets that have an indefinite useful life, the recoverable amount is estimated at each
              reporting date.                                                     
              An assessment is made at each reporting date to determine whether there is an indication that previously recognised
              impairment losses no longer exist or have decreased. If such indication exists, the asset’s or CGU’s recoverable amount is
              estimated.                                                          
              Where an impairment loss subsequently reverses, the carrying amount of an asset (or CGU) is increased to the revised
              estimate of its recoverable amount. This is done so that the increased carrying amount does not exceed the carrying
              amount that would have been determined had no impairment loss been recognised for the asset (or CGU) in prior years.
              A reversal of an impairment loss is recognised immediately in profit or loss. For goodwill and intangible assets that have
              an indefinite useful life, the recoverable amount is estimated at each reporting date. Whenever the carrying amount of
              an asset or its CGU exceeds its recoverable amount, an impairment loss is recognised in profit or loss. As goodwill is not
              capable of generating cash flows independently of other assets, in assessing the recoverable amount of goodwill, it is
              allocated to CGUs on a reasonable and consistent basis. The recoverable amount of the CGU (including an allocation of
              goodwill) is assessed with reference to the future cash flows of the CGU. Where an impairment is identified for a CGU,
              the impairment is applied first to the goodwill allocated to the CGU and then to other assets on a pro rata basis
              comprising the CGU, provided that each identifiable asset is not reduced to below its recoverable amount. Any
              impairment of goodwill will not be subsequently reversed.           
           3.4 Common control reserve                                             
              Common control transactions are accounted for using the pooling of interest method with the difference between the
              carrying amount of the transferring entity and consideration recognised in a separate reserve in equity. Comparative
              information is restated where relevant.                             
           3.5 Other reserves                                                     
              Other reserves relates to equity that is non-operating in nature, for example repurchase of shares, common control
              reserve, share-based payments and foreign currency translation reserve.

           3.6 Significant accounting estimates, judgements and assumptions       
                                                                                  
              The presentation of the results of operations, financial position and cash flows in these annual financial statements of the
              Group is dependent upon and sensitive to the accounting policies, assumptions and estimates that are used as a basis
              for the preparation of these financial statements. Management has made certain judgements in the process of applying
              the Group’s accounting policies. These, together with the key assumptions concerning the future, and other key sources
              of the estimation uncertainty at the reporting date, are discussed. 
              Advertising agreements                                              
              The Group enters into cooperative advertising agreements with its suppliers. A cooperative advertising agreement
              provides that the manufacturer will participate in the advertising cost of the Group. Significant judgement is required to
              determine whether the reimbursement of advertising costs received by the Group from the manufacturer should be
              accounted for as other income or as a reduction against cost of sales. The Group accounts for the reimbursement as part
              of 'other income' when both of the following criteria are met:      
              • The manufacturer receives, or will receive, an identifiable advertising service in exchange for the reimbursement. In
                order to meet this condition, the advertising service must be sufficiently separable from the Group’s purchase of the
                manufacturer’s products such that the manufacturer could have entered into an exchange transaction with a party
                other than a purchaser of its products or services in order to receive that advertising service.
              •                                                                   
                The Group can reasonably estimate the fair value of the advertising services. If the amount of reimbursement paid by
                the manufacturer exceeds the estimated fair value of the advertisement services, that excess amount is characterised
                as a reduction of cost of sales when recognised in the Group’s statement of comprehensive income.
              Ownership of Dis-Chem Oncology                                      
              The group owns 50% of the share capital of Dis-Chem Oncology Proprietary Limited (which owns 100% of Eton Road
              Proprietary Limited) but due to the ability to appoint the majority of directors and control the operations of Oncology,
              the company is consolidated by the Group.                           
              Deferred tax assets – assessed losses                               
              Deferred tax assets are raised to the extent that it is probable that future taxable profits will be available against which the
              unused tax losses can be utilised. The assessment of future taxable profits is based on forecasted results and the
              application of existing tax laws. The inputs of forecasted results (such as growth rates, margins and expenditure) align
              with the Group’s annual budgets approved by executive management. To the extent that future results differ significantly
              from estimates, the ability to realise the deferred tax assets could be impacted.
           3.7 New and amended standards and interpretations effective for the period ended
              28 February 2026                                                    
              The following new or revised standards became effective in the current period but had no significant impact on the
              financial position or performance of the Group or company but additional disclosure has been given where necessary:
              • Illustrative Examples on IFRS 7, IFRS 18, IAS 1, IAS 8, IAS 36 and IAS 37. This had no impact on the group or
                company. The group and company does not operate in a high-risk industry from a climate transition perspective and
                it is unlikely that renewable energy technology advancements, climate-related consumer preferences, climate-
                related legislation, or reputational damage will impact the group or company. The group and company is not a high
                greenhouse gases emitter or fossil fuel producer, nor does the group or company provide extensive credit to
                customers that could be subject to climate change risk of non-payment. Furthermore, the group and company has
                not suffered significant physical climate change-related losses in recent years (i.e. those caused by floods, bush fires,
                drought etc.). This means that future projected cashflows used in cash generating unit value-in-use impairment
                assessments is unlikely to require climate-related considerations in their quantification.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) are present in this capture.** The pages are continuous policy text with no table footnotes. No missing-footnote verification is required for this section.

- **Advertising-agreement judgement (note 3.6)** `[D003, p. 20]`: This is the most forecast-relevant qualification. Reimbursements from suppliers are split: (a) recognised as **other income** only where the manufacturer receives an identifiable, separable advertising service and the Group can reasonably estimate fair value; (b) any **excess over estimated fair value is a reduction of cost of sales**. Implication: gross margin and other income are both sensitive to management's fair-value estimate of advertising services — a reclassification between the two lines is possible without changing operating profit. Must be verified against Note 3.6/8/16 amounts (Q-9348bd1461904198, Q-a99837e8ec864376).

- **Dis-Chem Oncology control judgement (note 3.6)** `[D003, p. 20]`: 50% shareholding but consolidated because the Group appoints the majority of directors and controls operations. Implication: 100% of Oncology revenue/EBITDA is consolidated with a 50% NCI attribution; forecasters must not treat it as an equity-accounted JV. Verify Oncology contribution and NCI share in segment/NCI notes (D005).

- **Deferred tax assets on assessed losses (note 3.6)** `[D003, p. 20]`: Recognition depends on forecast taxable profits aligned to executive-approved budgets (growth rates, margins, expenditure). Implication: a forecast downgrade could trigger DTA derecognition and a tax-charge spike. Verify DTA balance and unrecognised assessed losses in the tax note (D005, Note 27.3).

- **Impairment testing basis (note 3.3)** `[D003, p. 19]`: Value-in-use uses **five-year management-account cash flows** at a pre-tax discount rate; goodwill impairment is not reversible. Implication: goodwill/intangibles carrying values depend on the same budgets underpinning the forecast — check goodwill balance and any FY2026 impairment in D005.

- **Climate-change qualification (note 3.7)** `[D003, p. 20]`: Management asserts the Group is not a high-risk climate industry, not a high GHG emitter/fossil-fuel producer, does not provide extensive credit exposed to climate non-payment risk, and has suffered no significant physical climate losses — therefore CGU value-in-use cash flows need no climate adjustment. This is a forward-looking assertion to test against the credit book (debtors) and store footprint in D005.

- **Common control reserve / other reserves (notes 3.4–3.5)** `[D003, p. 19]`: Other reserves = non-operating equity (share repurchases, common control reserve, share-based payments, foreign currency translation). Relevant to Q-5b5774e8e3f243a8 (composition of R4,566,716k other reserves) — the policy confirms the categories but not the split.

### 2. Footnote & Commentary Unpacking

**Footnote (1) — D-Chem Proprietary Limited (D003, p. 24):** "The Company has a 50% interest in D-Chem Proprietary Limited, a joint venture. The Company's share of the profit/(loss) of D-Chem Proprietary Limited for the year ended 28 February 2026 is R(1.2) million (2025: R(1.4) million)." This is a joint venture, not a subsidiary, and is equity-accounted. The loss is small and consistent year-over-year. No forecast impact beyond the equity-accounted line.

**Footnote (2) — Dis-Chem Life Proprietary Limited (D003, p. 25):** "The Group acquired a 50% interest in the ordinary share capital of Dis-Chem Life Proprietary Limited for a consideration of R155.9 million. Dis-Chem Life is at the forefront of life insurance innovation and utilizing advanced AI, and proprietary technology, and has created a revolutionary offering that transforms the traditional insurance experience. The company's principal place of business is in South Africa. In the current financial period an additional R189 million was acquired in preference shares." This is a significant disclosure. The Group acquired 50% of Dis-Chem Life for R155.9m, and then injected a further R189m in preference shares during FY2026. The summarised financial information (p. 26) shows Dis-Chem Life made a **loss of R100.4 million** in FY2026 (2025: loss of R115.6 million), with the Group's share of loss at R50.2 million (2025: R29.4 million). Revenue was R85.3 million (2025: R28.8 million). This is a loss-making joint venture that is consuming cash (R189m preference share investment) and generating equity-accounted losses. **Forecast implication:** The R189m preference share investment is a cash outflow that needs to be verified in the cash flow statement (D002/D004). The R50.2m share of loss is a drag on group HEPS. The revenue growth from R28.8m to R85.3m suggests scaling, but the loss widened. This needs to be tracked for FY2027 — is there a path to profitability, or is this a continuing cash drain?

**Footnote (3) — Kaelo Holdings Proprietary Limited (D003, p. 25):** "Kaelo houses a complementary portfolio of health assets, including benefit-rich gap and primary health insurance products, occupational health clinics, and is the owner of the AskNelson psychological wellbeing platform. Kaelo's principal place of business is in South Africa." The summarised financial information shows Kaelo revenue of R1,383.1m (2025: R1,181.4m), profit of R108.7m (2025: R54.1m), and the Group's share of profit at R27.2 million (2025: R13.5 million). This is a profitable associate with growing contributions. The Group holds 25%. The carrying value is R235.7 million (2025: R208.6 million). This is a positive contributor to equity-accounted income and should be factored into the forecast as a growing, profitable associate.

**Note 4 — Subsidiaries (D003, pp. 23-24):** The subsidiary list shows several changes in equity interest:
- **Dis-Chem Airport Junction Proprietary Limited**: 90.0% (2025: 80.0%) — increased ownership
- **Dis-Chem Gallo Shopping Centre Francistown Proprietary Limited**: 85.0% (2025: 80.0%) — increased ownership
- **Healthforce Proprietary Limited**: 100.0% (2025: 87.5%) — increased to full ownership

**Key observation**: The note states "There were no material non-controlling interests identified within the Group in the current and prior financial period. The Group assesses the share of non-controlling interest in profit after tax to be material if the interest is higher than 10% (2025: 10%) of consolidated profit after tax." This is a significant statement — it means NCI is immaterial to the group's profit. However, the group has numerous subsidiaries with less than 100% ownership (e.g., Dis-Chem Ballito Junction 75%, Dis-Chem Krugersdorp 51%, Dis-Chem Three Rivers 75%, etc.). The fact that NCI is deemed immaterial suggests these subsidiaries are small relative to the group. This should be verified against the NCI balance in the balance sheet (D002/D004).

**Note 5 — Associates and Joint Ventures (D003, p. 25):**
- **Kaelo Holdings**: 25% interest, carrying value R235,746k (2025: R208,576k). Share of profit R27,169k (2025: R13,531k). Revenue R1,383,142k (2025: R1,181,424k). Profit R108,676k (2025: R54,124k). This is a growing, profitable associate.
- **Dis-Chem Life Proprietary Limited**: 50% interest, carrying value R265,323k (2025: R126,508k). Share of loss R(50,186)k (2025: R(29,432)k). Revenue R85,338k (2025: R28,789k). Loss R(100,372)k (2025: R(115,609)k). The carrying value increased from R126.5m to R265.3k — this is due to the R189m preference share acquisition plus the share of losses. The loss is narrowing slightly but still substantial.
- **Other associates/JVs**: R63,024k (2025: R21,183k). The note states: "The Group's share of profit/total comprehensive profit of associates (excluding Kaelo) is R31.8 million (2025: loss of R3.9 million) and profit of joint ventures (excluding Dis-Chem Life) is R39.4 million (2025: R40 million)."

**Total investments in associates and joint ventures**: R564,093k (2025: R356,267k), an increase of R207,826k (+58.3%). This is driven by:
- Kaelo: +R27,170k (share of profit)
- Dis-Chem Life: +R138,815k (R189m preference shares less R50.2m share of loss)
- Other: +R41,841k

The R189m preference share investment in Dis-Chem Life is a significant capital allocation decision. It is a cash outflow that does not appear as an acquisition of a subsidiary (it's an associate/JV), so it will be in investing activities as "investment in associates/joint ventures" or similar. This needs to be verified in the cash flow statement (D002/D004).

**Note 3.8 — New and amended standards (D003, pp. 21-22):** The Group has not early-adopted any new standards. The key upcoming standard is IFRS 18 (effective 1 January 2027), which will change the presentation of the income statement and cash flow statement. Specifically:
- Operating profit must be the starting point for indirect method cash flows.
- Dividends paid will be classified as financing activities (currently likely in operating or financing depending on policy).
- Interest paid – financing activity; interest received – investing activity.
- Management-defined performance measures (like HEPS) will require additional disclosure.

This is a forward-looking disclosure that will affect FY2027 reporting (the year ending Feb 2027). For forecasting purposes, the FY2026 numbers are on the old basis. The FY2027 statements will be restated/re-presented under IFRS 18. This is a disclosure/layout change, not a change in accounting principles, so the underlying economics are unchanged. However, the classification of dividends paid and interest may change, which affects free cash flow definitions. This is relevant for Q-9c499ce17c37452f (dividends paid classification).

### 2. Footnote & Commentary Unpacking

**Footnote (1) — D-Chem Proprietary Limited (D003, p. 24):** "The Company has a 50% interest in D-Chem Proprietary Limited, a joint venture. The Company's share of the profit/(loss) of D-Chem Proprietary Limited for the year ended 28 February 2026 is R(1.2) million (2025: R(1.4) million)." This is a joint venture, not a subsidiary, and is equity-accounted. The loss is small and consistent year-over-year. No forecast impact beyond the equity-accounted line.

**Footnote (2) — Dis-Chem Life Proprietary Limited (D003, p. 25):** "The Group acquired a 50% interest in the ordinary share capital of Dis-Chem Life Proprietary Limited for a consideration of R155.9 million. Dis-Chem Life is at the forefront of life insurance innovation and utilizing advanced AI, and proprietary technology, and has created a revolutionary offering that transforms the traditional insurance experience. The company's principal place of business is in South Africa. In the current financial period an additional R189 million was acquired in preference shares." This is a significant footnote. The Group acquired 50% of Dis-Chem Life for R155.9m, and in FY2026 acquired an additional R189m in preference shares. The summarised financial information (p. 26) shows Dis-Chem Life's revenue grew from R28.8m to R85.3m, but its loss deepened from R115.6m to R100.4m (slightly improved). The Group's share of loss is R50.2m (2025: R29.4m). The carrying value of the investment increased from R126.5m to R265.3m, reflecting the R189m preference share injection less the R50.2m share of loss. This is a loss-making associate that is consuming cash. The R189m preference share investment is a cash outflow that must be verified in the cash flow statement (D002/D004). The question is whether this investment is expected to generate returns or is a cash drain.

**Footnote (3) — Kaelo Holdings Proprietary Limited (D003, p. 25):** "Kaelo houses a complementary portfolio of health assets, including benefit-rich gap and primary health insurance products, occupational health clinics, and is the owner of the AskNelson psychological wellbeing platform. Kaelo's principal place of business is in South Africa." Kaelo's revenue grew from R1,181.4m to R1,383.1m (+17.1%), and profit more than doubled from R54.1m to R108.7m. The Group's share of profit increased from R13.5m to R27.2m. This is a strong performer and a positive contributor to equity-accounted income. The carrying value increased from R208.6m to R235.7k. This is a good news story and should be factored into the forecast as a growing associate contribution.

**Note 4 — Subsidiaries (D003, pp. 23-24):** The footnote (2) states: "During the period, the Group acquired interest in certain companies. Refer to note 27.4." This refers to the following subsidiaries where equity interest increased:
- Dis-Chem Airport Junction Proprietary Limited: 90.0% (2025: 80.0%)
- Dis-Chem Gallo Shopping Centre Francistown Proprietary Limited: 85.0 (2025: 80.0)
- Healthforce Proprietary Limited: 100.0 (2025: 87.5)
- Dis-Chem The Fields Proprietary Limited: 85.0 (2025: 80.0)
- The Pharmacy Development Academy Proprietary Limited: 100.0 (2025: 70.0)
- Dis-Chem Game City Proprietary Limited: 85.0 (2025: n/a) — new
- I Watson Proprietary Limited (note 5): 100.0 (2025: n/a) — new
- Smart Cart Proprietary Limited: 100.0 (2025: n/a) — new
- Eton Road Proprietary Limited: 50.0 (2025: n/a) — new, 50% but consolidated

Footnote (3) lists companies deregistered during the period: Dis-Chem Festival Mall, Dis-Chem Rynfield Terrace Pharmacy, Dis-Chem Maponya Mall Pharmacy, Dis-Chem York Street Pharmacy, Dis-Chem Ferndale Mall Pharmacy, The Local Choice Scott Street, LJ Farrel and Sons, Pure MD Services, Superstrike Investment 56. These deregistrations are administrative and likely have no material financial impact, but they should be verified as not masking store closures or disposals.

The note states: "There were no material non-controlling interests identified within the Group in the current and prior financial period. The Group assesses the share of non-controlling interest in profit after tax to be material if the interest is higher than 10% (2025: 10%) of consolidated profit after tax." This is a significant statement. It implies that despite having subsidiaries with 51%, 65%, 70%, 71%, 72%, 75%, 85%, 90%, 95% ownership, the NCI share of profit is less than 10% of consolidated profit after tax. This needs to be verified against the actual NCI balance and NCI share of profit in the financial statements (D002/D005). If NCI is truly immaterial, then the non-wholly-owned subsidiaries are small relative to the group. But if NCI is material and this statement is incorrect, it could be a red flag.

        6. Segmental information                                                  
                                                                                  
           An operating segment is defined as a component of an entity that engages in business activities from which it may earn
           revenues and incur expenses whose operating results are regularly reviewed by the entity’s chief operating decision-maker,
           being the executive directors, in order to make decisions about resources to be allocated to the segment and assess its
           performance and for which discrete financial information is available. 
           The Group has identified two reportable segments. The following describes the operations in each of the reportable
           segments:                                                              
           Retail                                                                 
           Retail consists of the Dis-Chem stores, retailers of pharmaceutical and a variety of health and beauty products, as well as
           pharma-logistic services and oncology and retailers of pharmaceutical products. All retail stores have been aggregated into
           one segment as they have similar economic characteristics (gross margins), products and services, type of customer and
           distribution methods.                                                  
           Baby is included in the retail operating segment as its operating results are not separately reviewed to make resourcing
           decisions. The expenses are incurred across the retail segment.        
           Wholesale                                                              
           Wholesale consists of the CJ Wholesale and Dis-Chem Distribution businesses, wholesalers of pharmaceutical and a variety
           of health and beauty products. The wholesale subsidiaries have been aggregated into one segment as they have similar
           economic characteristics (gross margins), products and services, type of customer and distribution methods.
           There are no external customers that account for more than 10% of the Group’s revenue in the current and prior financial
           year.                                                                  
           Geographic information                                                 
           With the exception of three stores in Namibia and four stores in Botswana, the Group operates in one principal geographical
           area, that being South Africa. The revenue, assets and liabilities recognised in non-South African countries are not significant
           and therefore do not form a separate segment.

7. Revenue from contracts with customers
Revenue from contracts with customers is predominantly derived from the sale of products through our retail stores and
warehouse channels.
SSaallee  ooff  ggooooddss  ––  wwhhoolleessaallee:: The Group sells a range of pharmaceutical, health and front shop products in the wholesale
market. Sales are recognised when control of the products has transferred, being when the products are delivered to the
customer. Delivery occurs when the products have been delivered to the specific location, the risks of obsolescence and loss
have been transferred to the customer, and either the customer has accepted the products in accordance with the sales
contract, the acceptance provisions have lapsed, or the Group has objective evidence that all criteria for acceptance have
been satisfied. A right to return liability (included in trade and other payables) and related asset (included in trade and other
receivables) are recognised for any expected returns that may take place within the Group’s return policy in relation to sales
made until the end of the reporting period. Accumulated experience is used to estimate such returns at the time of sale at a
portfolio level (expected value method). No element of financing is deemed present as the sales are made with a credit term
of 30 to 60 days, which is consistent with market practice.
SSaallee  ooff  ggooooddss  ––  rreettaaiill:: The Group operates a chain of retail stores selling pharmaceutical, health and front shop products.
Revenue from the sale of goods is recognised when products are sold to the customer. Payment of the transaction price is
due immediately when the customer purchases the products and takes delivery in store. It is the Group’s policy to sell certain
of its products to the customer with a right of return of between 10 to 30 days depending on the specific product. Legally
returns on dispensary items are prohibited. Therefore, a right to return liability (included in trade and other payables) and
related asset (included in trade and other receivables) are  recognised for the products expected to be returned, that may
take place within the Group's return policy. Accumulated experience is used to estimate such returns at the time of sale at a
portfolio level (expected value method).
CCuussttoommeerr  llooyyaallttyy  pprrooggrraammmmee:: The Group operates a loyalty scheme which allows retail customers to accumulate points that
entitle them, subject to certain criteria, to use these points in the future in any store in exchange for goods or services. A
contract liability for the award points is recognised at the time of the sale and revenue is recognised when the points are
redeemed taking into account breakage, if any (refer to note 26). The point system came to an end in the current financial
period and was replaced with direct discounts at point of sale.

8. Profit before taxation
Advertising and marketing income, data and administration fees as well as franchise fees are recognised over time when the
service is provided to the vendor, as the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefit provided.
Commission income is recognised on a monthly basis as earned.
The cost of employee benefits is recognised as an expense during the period in which the employee renders the service.

9. Net financing costs
Finance income
Finance income is recognised utilising the effective interest method, being the rate that exactly discounts the estimated
future cash receipts over the expected life of the financial instrument or a shorter period, where appropriate, to the net
carrying amount of the financial asset. Interest income is included in finance income in profit or loss.
Finance costs
All borrowing costs are recognised in profit or loss using the effective interest method as there are no qualifying assets.

### 1. Answers to Section-Specific Questions (D003)

**Q-3a1a1a1a (from Q-0a1a1a1a) — What is the nature and financial impact of the I-D-Chem acquisition?**
- **Status**: Resolved
- **Evidence & Answer**: The Group acquired 100% of I-Dis-Chem (Pty) Ltd on 1 August 2025 for R26.7 million (cash paid R29.1m, net of R5.6m cash acquired). The acquisition contributed R26.2m revenue and R0.3m profit before tax from the date of acquisition. If acquired at the beginning of the year, it would have contributed R46.3m revenue and R0.5m PBT. Goodwill of R22.4m was recognised, comprising expected synergies from expanded product/clinic offerings and trade term agreements. The fair value of identifiable net assets was R6.7m, including R2.0m inventory and R0.4m receivables (gross contractual amount expected to be fully received). Acquisition-related costs were expensed. [D003, physical PDF p. 27]

**Q-4a1a1a1a — What are the Group's reportable segments and their financial performance?**
- **Status**: Resolved
- **Evidence & Answer**: The Group has two reportable segments: Retail (Dis-Chem stores, pharma-logistic services, oncology) and Wholesale (CJ Wholesale, Dis-Chem Distribution). For FY2026:
  - **Retail**: External revenue R36,592.3m; gross profit R8,032.4m (21.95% margin); EBITDA R2,664.3m (7.3% margin); operating profit R1,465.8m (4.0% margin); capex R1,020.4m; total assets R13,950.0m.
  - **Wholesale**: External revenue R6,233.4m; gross profit R1,985.5m (31.85% margin on external+inter-segment revenue of R34,044.3m); EBITDA R471.2m (1.4% margin); operating profit R361.7m (1.1% margin); capex R83.2m; total assets R11,670.4m.
  - **Group**: Revenue R42,825.8m; gross profit R9,409.2m (21.97%); EBITDA R3,161.0m (7.4%); operating profit R1,853.1m (4.3%); PBT R1,394.7m.
  - **FY2025 comparatives**: Group revenue R39,172.3m; gross profit R8,800.4m (22.47%); EBITDA R3,269.5m (8.3%); operating profit R2,104.1m (5.4%); PBT R1,633.7m.
  - **Geographic**: Three stores in Namibia, four in Botswana; non-SA revenue/assets/liabilities not significant. No external customer >10% of Group revenue. [D003, physical PDF pp. 28–30]

**Q-5a1a1a1a — What are the material items included in other income and expenses by segment?**
- **Status**: Resolved
- **Evidence & Answer**: Material items (≥10% of consolidated PBT) for FY2026:
  - **Retail other income**: Advertising and marketing income R1,475.8m; Data and administration fees R1,641.4m.
  - **Wholesale other income**: Data and administration fees R376.3m.
  - **Retail other expenses**: Computer R608.3m; Advertising R704.6m; Consulting R276.2m; Commission R210.5m; Courier R181.5m; Occupancy R688.4m; Employee benefits R5,221.3m; Security R156.9m.
  - **Wholesale other expenses**: Courier R237.1m; Employee benefits R798.9m; Service fee paid R642.1m.
  - **FY2025 comparatives**: Retail advertising/marketing income R1,234.1m; data/admin fees R1,405.3m; profit on IFRS 16 release R103.7m; Retail employee benefits R4,681.4m; Wholesale service fee R566.9m. [D003, physical PDF pp. 29–30]

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Footnote (1) on p. 27 — Trade and other receivables fair value**
- **Quote**: "The carrying amount reflects the gross contractual amounts receivable and we expected to receive the full amount at date of acquisition."
- **Implication**: No ECL allowance was recognised on the R396k receivables acquired with I-Dis-Chem. This is a small balance but signals management's confidence in collectability at acquisition date. Must verify in Note 17 (D005/D006) whether any post-acquisition impairment has been recognised on these receivables.

**Footnote (1) on p. 29 — Material items threshold**
- **Quote**: "Items are only disclosed if material in that segment, based on 10% of consolidated profit before tax."
- **Implication**: The segmental material items table is **incomplete by design** — only items exceeding 10% of consolidated PBT (R139.5m) are shown. This means smaller but potentially important cost lines (e.g., IT, professional fees, travel) are omitted. The R10,093.5m "Other expenses (excluding depreciation and amortisation)" line in the segment table is therefore not fully decomposed. Must verify in Note 8 (D005/D006) whether the full other expenses breakdown reconciles to this R10,093.5m figure.

**Footnote (1) on p. 32 — Lease payments**
- **Quote**: "Lease payments relate to variable lease payments of R4.7 million (2025: R2.6 million) in the Group and R0.8 million (2025: R0.7 million) in the company not included in the measurement of lease liabilities (for example, turnover based rental) and R163 million (2025: R86 million) in Group and R65.6 million (2025: R57.1 million) in company relating to short-term leases. There was no expense in the current or prior period relating to low-value assets."
- **Implication**: Short-term lease costs nearly doubled (R86m → R163m), suggesting either more short-term lease arrangements or a change in lease terms. Variable lease payments also increased (R2.6m → R4.7m), potentially indicating turnover-linked rental agreements. These are **not** included in IFRS 16 lease liabilities and therefore represent off-balance-sheet occupancy costs. Must verify in Note 22 (D005/D006) the total lease liability, ROU depreciation, and lease finance charges to reconcile the full occupancy cost picture.

**Loyalty programme note (p. 31)**
- **Quote**: "The point system came to an end in the current financial period and was replaced with direct discounts at point of sale."
- **Implication**: The contract liability for loyalty points (Note 26) should have been released to revenue in FY2026. This explains the 60.6% fall in deferred revenue from R86,912k to R34,242k (Q-b8bbff1173f34f0d). Must verify in Note 26 (D005/D006) that the release is fully accounted for and that no residual liability remains.

**Revenue recognition policy (p. 31)**
- **Quote**: "No element of financing is deemed present as the sales are made with a credit term of 30 to 60 days, which is consistent with market practice."
- **Implication**: Wholesale revenue is recognised at a point in time with no financing component. Retail revenue is recognised at point of sale. The policy does not explicitly address **customer financial services revenue** (finance charges, initiation fees, monthly service fees, credit life insurance) — this is a critical gap. Must verify in Note 7 (D005/D006) whether financial services revenue is included in the R42,825.8m revenue figure or disclosed separately.

**Finance costs policy (p. 33)**
- **Quote**: "All borrowing costs are recognised in profit or loss using the effective interest method as there are no qualifying assets."
- **Implication**: No borrowing costs were capitalised to inventory or PPE. This is consistent with a retail business but means all finance costs (R554.1m) flow through P&L. The lease liability finance charge of R252.4m is the largest component, followed by bank overdraft R145.7m and bank loans R155.8m. Must verify in Note 22/23 (D005/D006) the split between lease and loan interest to reconcile to cash finance costs paid (Q-8113f4ff41654e36).

        10. Taxation                                                              
                                                                                  
           Current tax                                                            
           Current tax assets and liabilities for the current and prior periods are measured at the amount expected to be recovered
           from or paid to taxation authorities. The tax rates and laws used to compute the amount are those that are enacted, or
           substantively enacted at the reporting date. Current income tax relating to items recognised directly in equity or other
           comprehensive income is recognised in equity or other comprehensive income and not in profit or loss. Management
           periodically evaluates positions taken in the tax returns where applicable tax regulations are subject to interpretation and
           establishes provisions where appropriate.                              
           Deferred tax                                                           
           Deferred taxation is provided using the liability method on all temporary differences between the tax bases of assets and
           liabilities and their carrying amounts at the reporting date. Deferred tax liabilities are recognised for all taxable temporary
           differences except:                                                    
           • in respect of taxable temporary differences associated with investments in subsidiaries and interests in associates and
             joint ventures, where the timing of the reversal of the temporary differences can be controlled and it is probable that the
             temporary differences will not reverse in the foreseeable future.    
           Deferred tax assets are recognised for all deductible temporary differences and unused tax losses, to the extent that it is
           probable that taxable profit will be available against which the deductible temporary differences and unused tax losses can
           be utilised:                                                           
           • in respect of deductible temporary differences associated with investments in subsidiaries and interests in associates and
             joint ventures, deferred tax assets are only recognised to the extent that it is probable that the temporary differences will
             reverse in the foreseeable future and taxable profit will be available against which the temporary differences can be
             utilised.
