        12. Property, plant and equipment                                         
           Property plant and equipment are stated at cost less accumulated depreciation and accumulated impairment. Property plant and
           equipment are depreciated on the straight-line basis at rates estimated to write each asset down to their residual value over the term of
           its useful life.                                                       
           Initial and subsequent costs are included in the asset’s carrying amount or are recognised as a separate asset, as appropriate, only
           when it is probable that future economic benefits associated with the item will flow to the Group/company and the cost of the item can
           be measured reliably. All other repairs and maintenance are charged to profit or loss during the financial period in which they are
           incurred.                                                              
           All assets are depreciated from the date they are available-for-use, on a straight-line basis, to allocate their cost to their residual value
           over their estimated useful life. Depreciation ceases at the earlier of either the date the asset is classified as held for sale or the date the
           asset is derecognised.                                                 
           The right-of-use (ROU) asset is measured based on the present value of the lease payments, initial direct costs incurred when entering
           in the lease less any lease incentives received. The ROU asset is depreciated over the shorter of the lease term or the useful life of the
           underlying asset.                                                      
           The estimated useful lives are as follows:                             
           – Land               Not depreciated                                   
           – Buildings          20 to 30 years                                    
           – Computer hardware  1 to 9 years                                      
           – Office and other equipment 1 to 10 years                             
           – Leasehold improvements 4 to 12 years                                 
           – Motor vehicles (owned) 1 to 10 years                                 
           – Furniture and fixtures 2 to 12 years                                 
           – Land and buildings (right-of-use) Lease term                         
           – Motor vehicles (right-of-use) Lease term                             
           – Equipment (right-of-use) Lease term                                  
           The residual values, useful lives and depreciation methods of property, plant and equipment are reviewed at each reporting date and
           adjusted if appropriate. At each reporting date it is assessed whether there is any indication that an asset may be impaired. If any such
           indication exists, the recoverable amount is estimated.                
           Where carrying values exceed the estimated recoverable amounts, tangible assets are written down to their recoverable amounts and
           the impairment is recognised in profit or loss immediately.            
           Please refer to note 3.3 on impairment of non-financial assets, where the recoverable amount is discussed.
           An asset is derecognised upon disposal or when no future economic benefits are expected from its use or disposal. Gains or losses on
           disposal are determined by comparing the proceeds with the carrying amount. These gains or losses are included in profit or loss in
           the period of derecognition.

Company charge R142,508k (2025: R193,218k). The cash-tax-paid reconciliation (R401,870k) is not in this capture — open for D005 Note 27.3.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **`*` footnote on the tax rate reconciliation** `[D003, physical PDF p. 35]`: "Other mainly includes **assessed losses not raised**, tax rate differences, sale of property, plant and equipment, dividends withholding tax and leave pay provision." This is the only place in the capture where unrecognised assessed losses are acknowledged. It means the 25.75% ETR is flattered/affected by a 0.32% "Other" bucket that mixes recurring items (leave pay, DWT) with non-recurring ones (assessed losses not raised, PPE disposals). **Forecast implication**: the FY2027 ETR should not be extrapolated mechanically from 25.75% — the recurring component needs isolating in the DTA note (D005). Also note the "Investment in associates and joint ventures" line of **(0.93)%** (2025: (0.33)%) — a non-deductible/equity-accounted tax drag that has nearly tripled; verify whether this is a permanent structural drag or a one-off (e.g. the JV intangible impairment of R18,324k being non-deductible).

- **IFRIC 23 qualification** `[D003, physical PDF p. 35]`: Management "assessed and concluded that the interpretation did not have an impact on its financial statements for the years presented" because "the Group does not operate in a complex multinational environment." This is a clean conclusion — no uncertain tax provision is carried. **Verification**: confirm in D005 that no uncertain-tax provision balance exists and that the cross-border operations (Namibia/Botswana/Eswatini per the subsidiary names in stored questions) are genuinely not "complex multinational."

- **Note 11 HEPS reconciliation — the R18,324k JV intangible impairment** `[D003, physical PDF p. 36]`: This is added back to arrive at headline earnings, so it is excluded from HEPS but **included in basic EPS**. It is the single largest reconciling item between EPS (114.2c) and HEPS (113.7c) and is non-recurring in nature (nil prior year). **Forecast implication**: FY2027 HEPS base should exclude it; but the impairment signals stress at a JV (likely Dis-Chem Life or Kaelo per stored questions) that needs identification in D005 Note 4/5.

- **Note 11 share roll-forward — treasury activity** `[D003, physical PDF p. 36]`: Treasury shares acquired (569,379) vs exercised (606,869) — net treasury release of 37,490 shares, a trivial net buyback in FY2026 versus FY2025's near-neutral (2,390,752 acquired vs 2,397,586 exercised). **Forecast implication**: no meaningful buyback capital allocation in FY2026; the 860,084,483 issued count is static, so DPS × 857.0m weighted shares is the correct dividend base.

- **Note 12 ROU depreciation policy** `[D003, physical PDF p. 37]`: ROU depreciated over the **shorter of lease term or useful life**, with land & buildings ROU over "Lease term." Combined with the stored lease liability of R2,943,233k, this confirms the IFRS 16 depreciation profile is lease-term-driven, not building-life-driven — relevant to the D005 Note 22 reconciliation of ROU depreciation vs lease finance charges.

- **Note 12 useful-life ranges** `[D003, physical PDF p. 37]`: Leasehold improvements 4–12 years, furniture & fixtures 2–12 years, computer hardware 1–9 years. The wide ranges imply judgement; no residual value or useful-life change disclosure in this capture — verify in D005 PPE note whether any useful-life/residual revisions occurred in FY2026.

- **Missing footnote check**: No footnote markers in this capture lack their definition text. The `*` marker on p.35 is fully defined on the same page.

13. Intangible assets
Intangible assets acquired separately are measured on initial recognition at cost. The cost of intangible assets acquired in a
business combination is its fair value as at the date of acquisition. Following initial recognition, intangible assets are carried at
cost less accumulated amortisation and accumulated impairment losses, if any. Internally generated intangible assets,
excluding capitalised development costs, are not capitalised and expenditure is reflected in profit or loss in the year in which
the expenditure is incurred.
The useful lives of intangible assets are assessed as either finite or indefinite. Intangible assets with finite lives are amortised
over the useful life and assessed for impairment whenever there is an indication that the intangible asset may be impaired.
The amortisation period and the amortisation method for an intangible asset with a finite useful life is reviewed at least at the
end of each reporting period. Changes in the expected useful life or the expected pattern of consumption of future economic
benefits embodied in the asset is accounted for by changing the amortisation period or method, as appropriate, and are
treated as changes in accounting estimates. The amortisation expense on intangible assets with finite lives is recognised in
profit or loss in the expense category consistent with the function of the intangible assets.
Intangible assets with indefinite useful lives (goodwill) are not amortised, but are tested for impairment annually, at the CGU
level. Impairment losses on goodwill are never reversed.
The estimated useful lives are as follows:

14. Deferred tax
The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed at each reporting date and reduced to the extent that it is no longer
probable that sufficient taxable profit will be available to allow all or part of the deferred tax asset to be utilised. Deferred tax
assets and liabilities are only offset if there is a legally enforceable right to offset current tax and the asset or liability relates to
the same taxation authority and the same taxable entity.
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the tax rates that are expected to apply to the period when the asset is
realised or the liability is settled, based on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted or substantively enacted at the
reporting date.
Also refer to accounting policy under note 10.

        16. Inventories                                                           
                                                                                  
           Inventories comprise merchandise for resale and are valued at the lower of cost determined on a weighted average moving
           cost basis and net realisable value. Net realisable value is the estimated selling price in the ordinary course of business, less
           estimated costs necessary to make the sale. The cost of merchandise sold includes normal shrinkage, wastage, inventory
           losses, trade discounts, rebates and other similar items. Obsolete and slow moving inventories are identified and written
           down to their net realisable value. The carrying amount of inventory is recognised as an expense in the period in which the
           related revenue is recognised.                                         
           The Group enters into various rebate agreements with its vendors in regards to the purchasing of inventory. These rebates
           are recorded as a reduction to the cost of the related inventory to the extent that the inventories have been sold, to the extent
           the inventory is unsold the rebates reduce the inventory balance. Certain of these agreements are based on the achievement
           of specific volumes of purchases over a specified period, including escalating rebates as certain pre-defined hurdles are met.
           The Group accrues these growth rebates at the point when it is probable that the hurdles will be met.

17. Trade and other receivables
Trade receivables are amounts due from medical aids and wholesale customers for merchandise sold or services rendered in
the ordinary course of business and are accounted for as financial assets at amortised cost in accordance with the accounting
policy disclosed in note 29. Prepayments are stated at their nominal values.
Expenses and assets are recognised net of VAT, except:
• when the VAT incurred on a purchase of assets or services is not recoverable from SARS, in which case, the VAT is
recognised as part of the cost of acquisition of the asset or as part of the expense item, as applicable; and
• receivables and payables which are stated inclusive of VAT. The net amount of sales tax recoverable from, or payable to,
SARS is included as part of receivables or payables in the statement of financial position.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

**Note 13 — Intangible assets (physical p. 42–44)**
- Useful lives disclosed: computer software 2–10 yrs; brand value 10–30 yrs; distribution right 10–15 yrs; customer list 7 yrs; licences 10 yrs `[D003, physical PDF p. 42]`. Goodwill is indefinite-life, tested annually at CGU level, never reversed.
- **Arithmetic check (Group 2026 cost roll-forward)**: Opening 1,851,119 + additions 395,995 + acquisitions 22,399 − disposals (154,074) + FX 15 = **2,115,454** ✓ matches stated closing cost `[D003, physical PDF p. 42]`.
- **Arithmetic check (Group 2026 accumulated amortisation)**: Opening (403,062) + current charge (123,759) + disposals 152,197 + FX (7) = **(374,631)** ✓ matches stated closing `[D003, physical PDF p. 42]`.
- **Arithmetic check (Group 2026 net carrying amount)**: 2,115,454 − 374,631 = **1,740,823** ✓ matches stated `[D003, physical PDF p. 42]`.
- **Anomaly — disposals/scrapping of computer software**: Cost disposed R141,098k but accumulated amortisation released only R139,221k, implying a net book value disposed of ~R1,877k. Yet no gain/loss on disposal is visible in this capture. **Verification question raised** (see Q-new below).
- **Anomaly — customer list disposals**: Cost disposed R12,976k and accumulated amortisation released R12,976k — fully written-off asset scrapped, consistent with nil NBV. Benign.
- **Anomaly — goodwill acquisitions R22,399k**: Note 13 attributes this to "Acquisitions (note 5)" and note 14 (goodwill table, p. 44) attributes it to "I Watson (note 5)". This is the only goodwill addition in FY2026. **Verification question raised** on I Watson consideration and contribution (already covered by Q-9578a5bba18b476f).
- **Anomaly — brand value and distribution right**: No additions, no disposals, no FX in FY2026; only amortisation charge (R5,398k brand, R8,971k distribution right). Stable.
- **Company 2026 computer software disposals**: Cost disposed R139,967k, accumulated amortisation released R138,248k → NBV disposed ~R1,719k. Same pattern as Group. **Verification question raised** on disposal gain/loss.
- **Company 2026 goodwill**: R121,057k unchanged; no impairment. Company customer list R28,136k cost, R25,345k accumulated amortisation, R2,791k NBV — nearly fully amortised.

**Note 13 — Goodwill CGU table (physical p. 44)**
- **Arithmetic check**: Sum of listed CGU goodwill = 19,327+1,087+274+565+37,370+15,206+7,670+3,670+2,750+92,961+21,500+1,023+17,491+968+4,201+343,957+6,067+20,355+856+10,960+5,009+255,890+240+603+55,986+22,399 = **948,385** ✓ matches stated total `[D003, physical PDF p. 44]`.
- **Concentration risk**: Baby (R343,957k) and Pure Pharmacy Holdings (R255,890k) together = R599,847k = **63.2% of total goodwill**. Logistical Services R92,961k = 9.8%. **Verification question raised** on Baby and Pure Pharmacy CGU headroom sensitivity — management asserts "no reasonable change to a key assumption would result in carrying amount exceeding recoverable amount," which is a strong claim for a 63%-concentrated goodwill book.
- **Discount rate inconsistency**: Text states retail range "12.02% to 14.42% (2024:13.7% to 16.1%)" — the comparative is labelled **2024**, not 2025. This is either a typo or a genuine two-year comparative. **Verification question raised** `[D003, physical PDF p. 44]`.
- **Discount rate movement**: Wholesale pre-tax rate fell from 15.7% to 14.02% (−168bps); retail range narrowed and fell. Lower discount rate **increases** value-in-use, mechanically supporting the no-impairment conclusion. **Verification question raised** on whether the rate reduction is justified by risk-free rate/market movements or is a discretionary assumption easing.
- **Terminal growth**: 4% (2025: 4%) — unchanged, above long-run SA nominal GDP growth plausibly. **Verification question raised** on justification.

**Note 14 — Deferred tax (physical p. 45)**
- **Arithmetic check (Group balance roll-forward)**: Opening 12,086 + charge to P&L 13,265 + acquisition (9) = **25,342** ✓ matches stated closing `[D003, physical PDF p. 45]`.
- **Arithmetic check (Group DTA/DTL split)**: DTA 148,383 − DTL 123,041 = **25,342** ✓ matches `[D003, physical PDF p. 45]`.
- **Arithmetic check (Group composition)**: 74,286+4,554+143,619−5,854+69,290−191,011−75,679+6,137 = **25,342** ✓ matches `[D003, physical PDF p. 45]`.
- **Key disclosure — tax losses**: DTA raised on estimated tax losses R69,290k (2025: R79,787k) — **down R10,497k**. Total assessed losses R457m (2025: R384m), of which **R202m (2025: R88m) unrecognised** — unrecognised losses **more than doubled** (+R114m). This directly answers part of Q-fd3755ff98be4f01 and Q-64791be57c9f40a7: the DTA on assessed losses is R69.3m, unrecognised assessed losses R202m. **Verification question raised** on which entities hold the unrecognised losses and whether they are recurring.
- **Anomaly — deferred revenue and S24C allowance**: Fell from R20,183k to R4,554k (−R15,629k, −77%). This is a large swing. **Verification question raised** — is this a release to P&L (tax benefit) or a genuine reversal of the underlying temporary difference? Ties to Q-b8bbff1173f34f0d (deferred revenue contract liability fell 60.6%).
- **Anomaly — lease liability DTA**: R143,619k (2025: R134,665k) — rose R8,954k, consistent with IFRS 16 lease liability growth. Ties to Q-3990b3abd8b34753.
- **Anomaly — PPE DTL**: (R191,011k) (2025: (R199,095k)) — DTL reduced R8,084k, consistent with capex/accelerated tax depreciation unwinding.
- **Anomaly — intangible DTL**: (R75,679k) (2025: (R85,387k)) — reduced R9,708k, consistent with amortisation of acquired intangibles.
- **Footnote * "Other"**: "mainly relates to right of return asset and liability, expected credit loss and tax rate differences on foreign subsidiaries" — R6,137k (2025: R5,071k). This is the only footnote definition in this capture. It confirms ECL is a deferred tax component but does **not** quantify the ECL DTA. **Verification question raised** on ECL DTA amount.
- **80% assessed-loss set-off rule**: Disclosed — companies with assessed losses can set off max 80% of assessed losses (subject to R1m minimum) against taxable income. This constrains DTA utilisation and is a **forecast input** for FY2027 effective tax rate.

**Note 16 — Inventories (physical p. 47)**
- **Finished goods**: R7,908,461k (2025: R7,905,213k) — essentially flat (+R3,248k, +0.04%) despite revenue growth of +9.3%. **This is a major forecast signal**: inventory turn improved materially. **Verification question raised** on inventory days and whether the flat balance reflects genuine efficiency or a stock-out risk.
- **Cost of inventories recognised as cost of sales**: R33,416,598k (2025: R30,371,972k) = +10.0%. Compare to revenue +9.3% — COGS grew slightly faster than revenue, consistent with the gross margin decline from 22.47% to 21.97% noted in Q-3dd14b2a88a344b9. **Partially resolves Q-3dd14b2a88a344b9** on the COGS rand amount; the write-down/shrinkage/rebate split is still not fully quantified.
- **Provision for obsolete inventory**: R3m (2025: R4.0m) — **reduced R1m**. Very small relative to R7.9bn inventory (0.04%). **Verification question raised** — is a R3m provision adequate for a R7.9bn book, or is inventory risk under-provided?
- **Write-offs**: R15m (2025: R49m) — **down R34m (−69%)**. Company R6.5m (2025: R13.5m). No reversals in either year. **Verification question raised** — the sharp fall in write-offs alongside flat inventory and rising COGS is a positive signal but needs corroboration against shrinkage rates.
- **Rebate policy**: "recorded as a reduction to the cost of the related inventory to the extent that the inventories have been sold, to the extent the inventory is unsold the rebates reduce the inventory balance. Certain of these agreements are based on the achievement of specific volumes... The Group accrues these growth rebates at the point when it is probable that the hurdles will be met." This is the policy text relevant to Q-9348bd1461904198 and Q-4bfd19ac8ef14ea8. **It does not quantify** the rebate amounts split between COGS and inventory. **Verification question raised** — the rand split remains open for D005/D006.
- **No footnote markers** on this page — the commentary is inline, not footnoted.

**Note 17 — Trade and other receivables (physical p. 48)**
- **Arithmetic check (Group net trade receivables)**: 1,897,879 − 22,380 = **1,875,499** ✓ matches `[D003, physical PDF p. 48]`.
- **Arithmetic check (Group total receivables)**: 1,875,499+1,563,715+155,594+188,735+6,136+10,699+8,108 = **3,808,486** ✓ matches `[D003, physical PDF p. 48]`.
- **Arithmetic check (Group ECL allowance roll-forward)**: Opening (18,840) + utilised 5,600 + raised (9,140) = **(22,380)** ✓ matches `[D003, physical PDF p. 48]`.
- **Trade receivables growth**: R1,897,879k vs R1,602,861k = **+18.4%**, well ahead of revenue +9.3%. **This is a red flag** — receivables growing ~2x revenue growth. **Verification question raised** on debtor days and whether credit terms loosened.
- **ECL allowance**: R22,380k on gross trade receivables R1,897,879k = **1.18%** coverage (2025: R18,840k / R1,602,861k = 1.18%). Coverage ratio **unchanged** despite 18.4% receivables growth — **verification question raised** on whether ECL staging/model assumptions changed.
- **Allowance raised**: R9,140k (2025: R11,244k) — **down R2,104k** despite receivables growing 18.4%. **Verification question raised** — is this a provisioning release that flatters FY2026 earnings?
- **Other receivables**: R1,563,715k (2025: R1,405,195k) = +11.3%. Footnote: "consist of rebates, promotions and advertising and logistic fee receivables as well as other sundry receivables." This is the **rebate receivable** — directly relevant to Q-9348bd1461904198 and Q-4bfd19ac8ef14ea8. **Verification question raised** on the rebate receivable balance and whether it is collectible.
- **Accrued income**: R155,594k (2025: R101,022k) = **+54.0%** — large jump. **Verification question raised** on what drove this (likely rebate accruals).
- **Prepayments**: R188,735k (2025: R198,114k) — footnote: "mainly bonus advances and prepayment of IT licences." Stable.
- **Related parties**: R10,699k (2025: R8,553k) — small, ties to note 28.
- **Right of return asset**: R8,108k (2025: R12,679k) — reduced R4,571k, consistent with the deferred revenue/S24C DTA reduction noted above.
- **Trade receivables terms**: "non-interest-bearing and are generally on terms of 7 to 60 days." **This is a key credit metric** — 60-day terms on a R1.9bn book. **Verification question raised** on ageing beyond 60 days.
- **No satisfactory-paid % or collection rate disclosed** — these are credit-book metrics that would normally appear in a credit/risk note (D005), not here. **Verification question raised** for D005.

           NCI shareholders loans relate to loans with individuals that have non-controlling interest in subsidiary companies of the
           Group. They are non-interest bearing and must be repaid before any dividend is paid to the individual.
           Related party loans in the Group relate to loans given to BEESECDCP, Tony Ferguson, Sable and Dis-Chem Life (2025:
           including Nexus). The Tony Ferguson loan earns interest at prime, Sable at prime plus 0.5% and Dis-Chem Life at the average
           bank overdraft rate (2025: Nexus at prime). BEESECDCP is interest free. These loans are unsecured and are repayable on
           demand.                                                                
           TLC loans relate to loans given to TLC franchise stores and earn interest linked to prime. They are secured by the inventory
           held in the store and the operating licence and are repayable in 5 years.
           Other loans in the Group mainly relate to loans given to Uphawu and The Tailor that are in the cut and trim industry as well as
           loans given to The Leasing Specialists and Dunes Pharmacy (2025: including ASU, USN, Stem Cell and Phyto Health which
           were repaid in the current year). These loans are unsecured and repayable on demand. The USN loan earned interest at
           prime less 1%. The ASU, Stem Cell, Phyto Health, Uphawu, The Tailor, The Leasing Specialists and Dunes Pharmacy loans are
           interest free. Other loans in the company mainly relate to Uphawu, The Tailor and The Leasing Specialists (2025: including
           ASU).                                                                  
           Related party loans in the company includes a loan for R502 million that the company has given to Dis-Chem Distribution
           Proprietary Limited in 2023 in regards to the purchase of the new Longmeadow warehouse. This loan earns interest at JIBAR
           plus 1.3% and is repayable at the end of 3 years.                      
           The South African Reserve Bank has confirmed that JIBAR will cease on 31 December 2026, after which South Africa will
           transition to alternative reference rates. JIBAR is expected to be replaced by ZARONIA, a near risk free rate administered
           under the oversight of the South African Reserve Bank. Any margin adjustments required as part of the transition will be
           calibrated to replicate the equivalent JIBAR based pricing, such that there is no material impact on the overall interest rates
           agreed. The majority of the loan agreements already provide for the JIBAR rates to transition to ZARONIA, the remaining loan
           agreements will be amended before JIBAR ceases on 31 December 2026.    
           Non-current assets in the Group consist mainly of related party loans given to Tony Ferguson, Sable, Dis-Chem Life and a
           portion of the TLC loans. Non-current assets in the Company consist mainly of related party loans given to Tony Ferguson,
           Sable, Dis-Chem Life and Dis-Chem Distribution.                        
           Refer to note 29 on credit risk management of loans receivable.

           Share-based payments                                                   
           Employees (including senior executives) of the Group receive remuneration in the form of share-based payments, whereby
           employees render services as consideration for equity instruments (equity-settled transactions).
           Equity-settled transactions                                            
           The cost of equity-settled transactions is determined by the fair value at the date when the grant is made using an
           appropriate valuation model, further details of which are given below. 
           The cost is recognised in other expenses as part of employee benefits, together with a corresponding increase in equity
           (other reserves), over the period in which the service and, where applicable, the performance conditions are fulfilled (the
           vesting period). The cumulative expense recognised for equity-settled transactions at each reporting date until the vesting
           date reflects the extent to which the vesting period has expired and the Group’s best estimate of the number of equity
           instruments that will ultimately vest. The expense or credit in profit or loss for a period represents the movement in
           cumulative expense recognised as at the beginning and end of that period.
           The dilutive effect of outstanding options is reflected as additional share dilution in the computation of diluted earnings per
           share (refer to note 11).                                              
           Forfeitable Share Plan (FSP) – bonus shares                            
           Under the FSP fully-paid shares (bonus shares) of Dis-Chem Pharmacies Limited are granted to regional and head office
           managers/executives. As the grants are in Dis-Chem's own shares they are treated as equity-settled share-based payments.
           The shares are registered in employees' names on the grant date and held in a brokerage account on behalf of the
           employees until vesting (approximately 3 years), as long as they are still employed by the Company. These shares are held as
           treasury shares in the Company. Employees receive dividends and voting rights on these shares during the vesting period.
           Exercise of the shares takes place on the vesting date.                
           The fair value of the shares is the fair market value on the grant date due to the fact that the employees have full rights to all
           the dividends declared before the end of the vesting period.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Trade receivables >120 days qualification** [D003, physical PDF p. 49]: "Trade receivables over 120 days in the current and prior year are mainly on payment plans and have been meeting the payment requirements and therefore not 100% provided for at year-end." This is a forward-looking collectibility assertion. It supports the 18.7% (Group) / 92.9% (Company) ECL rates on the >120 day bucket rather than 100% provisioning. **What must be verified:** the satisfactory-paid % and collection rate in note 29, and whether the payment-plan population is growing (Group >120 day gross rose R84,300k → R94,593k, +12.2%). If payment-plan balances are growing while ECL coverage stays flat, the forecast debtor cost line is understated.

- **Pledged receivables qualification** [D003, physical PDF p. 49]: "Trade and other receivables relating to CJ Pharmaceutical Enterprises Limited amounting to R400 million (2025: R400 million) were pledged as security for the revolving overdraft facilities with Standard Bank. Under the pledge the bank can claim debtors' receipts if CJ defaults on the bank overdraft." This is a contingent encumbrance on R400m of receivables — material relative to Group gross trade receivables of R1,897,879k (~21%). **What must be verified:** CJ Pharmaceutical's relationship to the Group (subsidiary? associate?), the size of the revolving overdraft it secures, and whether the pledge restricts liquidity in a stress scenario. This affects the going-concern / covenant assessment (Q-740992ca8c3945a3, Q-4497778bcc6a42f2).

- **Loans receivable — related-party concentration** [D003, physical PDF p. 50]: Group related-party loans R111,510k (2025: R95,478k) to BEESECDCP, Tony Ferguson, Sable and Dis-Chem Life; Company related-party loans R949,376k (2025: R861,985k), including a R502m loan to Dis-Chem Distribution at JIBAR+1.3%, repayable at end of 3 years. These are unsecured and repayable on demand. **What must be verified:** impairment assessment on these related-party loans (note 29 credit risk), and whether the R502m Distribution loan is eliminated on consolidation (it should be, since Distribution is a subsidiary — confirm).

- **JIBAR transition qualification** [D003, physical PDF p. 50]: JIBAR ceases 31 Dec 2026, replaced by ZARONIA; "any margin adjustments required as part of the transition will be calibrated to replicate the equivalent JIBAR based pricing, such that there is no material impact on the overall interest rates agreed." This is a forward-looking claim about FY2027 finance costs. **What must be verified:** whether the R502m Distribution loan and other JIBAR-linked facilities have documented ZARONIA fallback language, and whether the "no material impact" assertion holds for the Group's external debt (loans payable R2,027,578k per stored context).

- **Treasury shares / FSP qualification** [D003, physical PDF pp. 51–53]: Treasury shares are held for the FSP and measured at cost. FY2026 treasury purchases of R60.4m (1,761,003 shares at R34.20) are material relative to the R123,237k closing treasury balance. The FSP expense was R35,337k (2025: R29,628k). **What must be verified:** whether the November 2025 buyback at R34.20 was an on-market buyback or FSP share purchase, and whether it is dilutive or anti-dilutive to HEPS. The 1,757,950 FSP shares granted 31 Aug 2025 (expiry 30 June 2028) will vest over ~3 years, creating a future share-based payment expense run-rate of roughly R12m/year (35,337/3) — relevant to FY2027–FY2029 other expenses.

- **Other reserves reconciliation tension** [D003, physical PDF p. 52]: Note 20 shows Group other reserves R4,689,953k, but the stored ledger (Q-5b5774e8e3f243a8) referenced R4,566,716k. The difference is R123,237k — exactly the treasury share balance. This suggests the earlier figure may have excluded treasury shares or used a different aggregation. **What must be verified:** the statement of changes in equity (D002/D005) to confirm which figure ties to the equity statement.

- **No footnote markers on these pages**: physical pp. 49–53 contain no `[^1]`-style footnote markers requiring definition lookup. The qualifications are inline narrative, addressed above.

22. Lease liability
At inception, the Group assesses whether a contract is or contains a lease. The Group recognises a right-of-use (ROU) asset
and lease liability at the commencement date of the lease.
The lease liability is measured at the present value of the lease payments net of cash lease incentives that are not paid at the
reporting date. Lease payments are apportioned between the finance charges and reduction of the lease liability using the
incremental borrowing rate to achieve a constant rate of interest on the remaining balance of the liability. Lease payments
for buildings exclude service fees and other costs.

Many of the store leases across the Group contain extension options. In many cases these terms are not reflected in
measuring the lease liabilities until management is reasonably certain they will be exercised. The Group considers all
relevant facts and circumstances that create an economic incentive to exercise, or not to exercise, the option, including any
expected changes in facts and circumstances from the commencement date until the exercise date of the option.
Future cash flow in the 2027 financial year relating to variable lease payments is expected to be approximately R2.7 million
for the Group and Rnil for the company (2025 financial year: R2.2 million  for the Group and Rnil for the company).

           The import supply chain finance programme allows Dis-Chem to make payments to foreign suppliers through a funding
           institution using a cloud-based system. Dis-Chem then receives extended terms of up to 150 days in which to make payment
           to said financial institution instead of prepaying the suppliers. As at 28 February 2026, R239 million (2025: R309 million) of the

           or a similar reference rate.                                           
           The South African Reserve Bank has confirmed that JIBAR will cease on 31 December 2026, after which South Africa will
           transition to alternative reference rates. JIBAR is expected to be replaced by ZARONIA, a near risk free rate administered
           under the oversight of the South African Reserve Bank. Any margin adjustments required as part of the transition will be
           calibrated to replicate the equivalent JIBAR based pricing, such that there is no material impact on the overall interest rates
           agreed. The majority of the loan agreements already provide for the JIBAR rates to transition to ZARONIA, the remaining loan
           agreements will be amended before JIBAR ceases on 31 December 2026.

        24. Trade and other payables                                              
                                                                                  
           Trade and other payables are obligations to pay for goods or services that have been acquired in the ordinary course of
           business from suppliers. They are accounted for as financial liabilities in accordance with the accounting policy disclosed in
           note 29.                                                               
           Expenses and assets are recognised net of VAT, except:

             recognised as part of the cost of acquisition of the asset or as part of the expense item, as applicable; and
           • receivables and payables which are stated inclusive of VAT. The net amount of sales tax recoverable from, or payable to,
             SARS is included as part of receivables or payables in the statement of financial position.

        25. Employee-related obligations                                          
                                                                                  
           Short-term employee obligations are measured at the undiscounted amount required to settle the present obligation at the
           reporting date. Included in short-term employee obligations are bonus and leave pay.
           The expected cost of short-term employee benefits are recognised in the form of paid absences as follows:
           • in the case of accumulating paid absences, when the employees render service that increases their entitlement to future
            paid absences; and                                                    
           • in the case of non-accumulating paid absences, when the absences occur.
           The expected cost of bonus payments are recognised when, and only when:
           • there is a present legal or constructive obligation to make such payments as a result of past events; and
           • a reliable estimate of the obligation can be made.                   
           A present obligation exists when, and only when, there is no realistic alternative but to make the payments.
           When an employee has rendered service to the Group during a period, the Group shall recognise the contribution payable
           to a defined contribution plan in exchange for that service as a liability (accrued expense), after deducting any contribution
           already paid. The expense is recognised in profit or loss.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Dividend footnote (1), p. 54**: "Declared subsequent to year-end on 28 May 2026 (2025: 29 May 2025). A final dividend of 15.92 cents per share was approved by the directors on 28 May 2026… subject to DWT rate of 20%… net dividend of 12.73 cents." Implication: the 15.9c final is a **non-adjusting subsequent event** — it is not a FY2026 liability at 28 Feb 2026, so FY2027 opening cash will absorb ~R137m (15.92c × ~861m shares) plus DWT leakage to non-exempt holders. The 15.92c vs table-rounded 15.9c is a rounding presentation, not a discrepancy. Verify in D005 Note 31 subsequent events and Note 21.

- **Lease liability note, p. 55**: "Many of the store leases… contain extension options. In many cases these terms are **not reflected in measuring the lease liabilities** until management is reasonably certain they will be exercised." Implication: the R2,943,233k liability **understates** the Group's true store-lease commitment; the R3,582,386k undiscounted minimum payments exclude optional renewal periods. This is a material off-balance-sheet store-footprint risk for FY2027+ rent escalation forecasting. Also: "Future cash flow in the 2027 financial year relating to variable lease payments is expected to be approximately R2.7 million for the Group" — immaterial turnover-linked rent, so rent is essentially fixed. No escalation rate disclosed — verify in D005/D006.

- **Loans payable note, p. 56**: "The South African Reserve Bank has confirmed that JIBAR will cease on 31 December 2026… The majority of the loan agreements already provide for the JIBAR rates to transition to ZARONIA, the remaining loan agreements will be amended before JIBAR ceases." Implication: **all** JIBAR-linked facilities (Absa R400m + R502m, Standard Bank bullet + R650m + R44m) reprice within FY2027; the "no material impact" claim is an assertion, not a quantified calibration. Also flag: **Standard Bank bullet matures 31 May 2027** — refinancing risk inside the forecast year. Supply Chain Finance R239m at SONIA-like rate is a **foreign-currency-linked** funding cost exposed to GBP/USD rates, not JIBAR.

- **Trade payables note, p. 57**: "Trade payables includes R965 million (2025: R784 million)… due to suppliers that have signed up to a supply chain financing programme… The Group assesses the arrangement against indicators… At 28 February, the payables met the criteria of trade payables as the value and terms of the liability payable has not changed and the Group has not given any security or incurred any additional costs." Implication: **reverse-factoring classification risk** — R965m (+23% YoY) sits in trade payables rather than borrowings; if a future auditor or lender reclassifies to debt, reported net debt and leverage covenants would deteriorate. This is a key forecast/covenant sensitivity. Verify in D005 Note 29 liquidity risk and any covenant note.

- **Employee obligations note, p. 58**: "The bonus is dependent on the Group performance as well as individual ratings." Bonus accrual R159,396k (2025: R142,660k), +11.7% — broadly in line with revenue growth; leave pay R168,875k (2025: R171,538k). No unusual qualification.

NOTES TO THE GROUP AND COMPANY
ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
for the year ended 28 February 2026
26. Deferred revenue (contract liability)
Deferred revenue liability is recognised for expected loyalty benefit points and gift vouchers redeemed by customers for
purchases made by participating customers for the loyalty points and gift vouchers purchased for cash during the last three
years, based on past experience of the level of redemptions. It is expected that a majority of these will be redeemed in the
next financial year and all will have been redeemed within two years of the reporting date. Assumptions used to calculate the
liability are based on current redemption rates at existing stores which are between 90% and 100% (2025: 90% and 100%).
Loyalty benefit point scheme
The Group operates a loyalty scheme which allows retail customers to accumulate points that entitle them, subject to certain
criteria, to use these points in the future in any store in exchange for goods or services. The transaction price is allocated to
the loyalty points with reference to the Rand value of the points and is deferred as a liability and recognised as revenue on
redemption of the points by customers. The Group experiences low levels of unredeemed loyalty points due to the ease
with which customers can redeem them at point of sale.
Gift vouchers
The fair value of gift vouchers which includes the expected redemption rate attributed to the vouchers, is deferred as a
liability and recognised as revenue on redemption of the gift vouchers by customers.

### 2. Footnote and Footnote Analysis

- **Footnote `*` (on the roll-forward tables)** — "Approximately 100% (2025: 100%) of the opening balance has been recognised as revenue in the current year." [D003, physical PDF p. 59]
  - **Implication**: The deferred revenue liability is effectively a one-year revolving balance — essentially all of each year's opening balance converts to revenue within 12 months. This means the R86,912k FY2025 opening balance was almost fully released in FY2026, and the R34,242k closing balance will largely reverse in FY2027. For forecasting, the revenue contribution from the opening balance is highly predictable (~100%), but the *level* of the closing balance depends on points/vouchers issued during the year.
  - **What must be verified**: Whether the collapse in loyalty points issued (R279,042k→R196,770k, −29.5%) reflects a change in the loyalty programme (e.g., points no longer issued, scheme redesign, or shift to instant discounts) or a change in accounting estimate. This materially affects FY2027 revenue recognition and the "other revenue" line.

- **Redemption-rate assumption** — "Assumptions used to calculate the liability are based on current redemption rates at existing stores which are between 90% and 100% (2025: 90% and 100%)." [D003, physical PDF p. 59]
  - **Implication**: The 90–100% redemption assumption is unchanged year-on-year, so the liability fall is not an estimate change — it is a volume/redemption-timing effect. The narrow 90–100% band leaves little estimation headroom; a shift to the low end would reduce the liability further.
  - **What must be verified**: Whether the "low levels of unredeemed loyalty points" statement is consistent with the near-zero closing loyalty balance (R3,053k) — i.e., is the scheme still economically meaningful, or is it being wound down?

- **Gift voucher fair value** — "The fair value of gift vouchers which includes the expected redemption rate attributed to the vouchers, is deferred as a liability…" [D003, physical PDF p. 59]
  - **Implication**: Gift voucher liability fell R31,646k→R22,296k (−29.5%), with vouchers issued R216,897k (2025: R229,016k) and revenue recognised R226,247k (2025: R229,304k). Issuance fell 5.3% while redemptions were broadly flat — a modest net drain. This is a small, stable line but worth monitoring for breakage assumptions.

- **Company vs Group loyalty divergence** — Company loyalty points closing balance is nil (2025: R52,516k) while Group is R3,053k (2025: R45,625k). [D003, physical PDF p. 59]
  - **Implication**: The Company recognised R292,714k of loyalty revenue against R240,198k issued (a R52,516k release), fully draining its liability. This suggests the loyalty scheme is now operated at Group/subsidiary level rather than in the Company entity — a structural shift that should be confirmed against the segment/entity notes.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) appear in this capture.** The page is a clean Note 27 table with no small-print qualifications. This is itself notable: the cash flow notes carry no explanatory caveats on the large working-capital swing or the deferred revenue release.
- **Opening qualification**: "Cash and cash equivalents are accounted for as financial assets at amortised cost and bank overdrafts are accounted for as financial liabilities in accordance with the accounting policy disclosed in note 29" [D004, physical PDF p. 60]. This confirms the overdraft is a **financial liability** (not netted as negative cash in the policy wording), which matters for the Note 27.5 reconciliation (cash R499,756k vs overdraft R1,666,720k → net negative R1,166,964k) — must be verified in D005.
- **"Amount on acquisition and take on (note 5)" R36,712k** in Note 27.3 [D004, physical PDF p. 60]: a tax provision assumed on acquisition, not cash consideration. Must be reconciled to Note 5 business combinations in D005 — do not confuse with the R23,475k business-combination cash outflow.
- **"Profit on IFRS 16 release on purchase of leased properties" nil in FY2026 (2025: (103,692)k)** [D004, physical PDF p. 60]: a large FY2025 non-cash one-off that flattered FY2025 cash generated from operations; its absence in FY2026 is a base-effect item for FY2027 forecasting.
- **"Loss on lease liability" R4,695k (2025: R8,001k)** [D004, physical PDF p. 60]: a non-cash lease remeasurement/termination item; needs to be tied to Note 22 lease movements in D005.
- **Company dividend income R135,887k (2025: R103,440k)** deducted in Note 27.1 [D004, physical PDF p. 60]: confirms intercompany dividends are eliminated at Group; the Group dividend **paid** line is not shown here.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Note 27.6 footnote (1), Group** [D005, physical PDF p. 62]: "The interest repaid on the lease liability is R252 million (2025: R253 million) and is reflected in finance costs under operating activities." This is the only explicit split of finance costs paid between lease and loan interest. It implies Group loan interest paid ≈ R559,644k − R252m ≈ R307.6m, but the exact loan-interest figure is not printed — verify against Note 23 and the finance-costs add-back of R554,066k. The FY2025 lease interest of R253m vs FY2026 R252m is essentially flat despite lease liability rising from R2,663,849k to R2,943,233k — worth checking whether the average rate fell or the timing of new leases skewed the charge.

- **Note 27.6 footnote (1), Company** [D005, physical PDF p. 62]: "The interest repaid on the lease liability is R201 million (2025: R161 million)." Company lease interest rose 25% while Group was flat — implies the Company absorbed a larger share of lease interest in FY2026, consistent with the Company lease liability rising from R2,033,694k to R2,349,702k. Verify whether intercompany lease arrangements explain the divergence.

- **Note 27.6 non-cash "Release/fair value changes" column**: Group lease liability shows R(20,796)k in FY2026 vs R(592,429)k in FY2025 — a 96% fall in lease releases. This is a material swing: FY2025 had large lease terminations/re-measurements that did not recur. Verify whether FY2025 included store closures or lease renegotiations that flattered the FY2026 comparative lease cost base.

- **Note 27.6 "New leases/transactions" column**: Group new leases R992,172k (2025: R824,373k), +20.4% — implies continued store rollout/renewals. Company new leases R817,865k (2025: R594,453k), +37.6%. This is a forward-looking signal of store expansion capex/lease commitments; verify against store count and trading-space disclosures.

- **Note 28 footnote (4) and Columbia Falls narrative** [D005, physical PDF p. 64]: "On 1 December 2024, the Group acquired 100% of the share capital of Columbia Falls for the purchase price of R519 million. This is a related party transaction due to the seller being an associate of certain directors and prescribed officers of Dis-Chem, who collectively are also material shareholders of Dis-Chem. This transaction was accounted for as an asset acquisition." This is a significant related-party asset acquisition (R519m) that is NOT in the FY2026 cash flow (it was FY2025) but explains the R40,188k interest expense in the FY2025 comparative and the R48,240k loan receivable from Columbia Falls at Company level in FY2026. Verify: (a) what assets were acquired (property/warehouse?), (b) whether the R519m is fair value, (c) whether the asset acquisition bypassed goodwill/impairment testing, and (d) the SENS announcement referenced.

- **Note 28 footnote on Dis-Chem Life** [D005, physical PDF p. 64]: "On 1 August 2024, the Group acquired a 50% interest in the ordinary share capital of Dis-Chem Life Proprietary Limited for a consideration of R155.9 million. Four Dis-Chem directors are indirect shareholders of the holding company of Dis-Chem Life Proprietary Limited and therefore the holding company is considered a related party to Dis-Chem." This confirms the R155.9m (not R189m as in some stored questions) JV consideration and the related-party nature. The R189m figure in stored questions may relate to a separate preference share investment — verify the distinction.

- **Note 28 footnote (1)** [D005, physical PDF pp. 63, 66]: "Relates to retail and warehouse space that is owned/partially owned by certain directors." Group lease liability to various property companies R106,805k (2025: R136,765k), interest expense R(10,100)k (2025: R(12,287)k). This is a director-linked lease commitment — verify whether lease terms are at market and whether these are included in the IFRS 16 lease liability of R2,943,233k.

- **Note 28 footnote (2)** [D005, physical PDF pp. 63, 64]: "Relates to associates and joint ventures of the Group as disclosed in note 4." Confirms which related parties are associates/JVs — useful for reconciling the associate/JV profit of R48,179k.

- **Note 28 footnote (3)** [D005, physical PDF pp. 63, 64]: "Relates to a company that is owned by certain directors." Bene purchases R42,909k (2025: R37,301k) — director-owned supplier.

- **Note 28 closing qualification** [D005, physical PDF p. 64]: "Related party receivable and payables are generally settled within 60 days." This is a soft qualification — verify whether any related-party balances are overdue beyond 60 days, especially the R949,376k Company loans receivable (which are clearly not trade and not 60-day).

- **Note 28 Group totals** [D005, physical PDF p. 63]: FY2026 loans receivable R111,510k, loans payable R37,517k, lease liability R106,805k, accounts receivable R10,699k, accounts payable R92,148k, interest income/(expense) R9,499k, purchases R502,034k, services received R405,357k. FY2025 comparatives: R95,478k / R39,307k / R136,765k / R8,553k / R47,568k / R(45,791)k / R420,410k / R317,158k. Note the interest line swung from R(45,791)k expense to R9,499k income — driven by Columbia Falls interest expense (R40,188k) not recurring and BEESECDCP/Sable/Tony Ferguson interest income continuing. Verify the swing is non-recurring.

- **Note 28 Company totals** [D005, physical PDF p. 66]: FY2026 loans receivable R949,376k, loans payable R991,529k, lease liability R106,805k, accounts receivable R245,172k, accounts payable R1,887,592k, interest R(37,848)k, sales R71,828k, purchases R20,753,320k, services received R1,043,921k. The R20.75bn Company purchases from related parties (mostly Dis-Chem Distribution R18.73bn and CJ Pharmaceutical R1.96bn) is the intercompany supply chain — verify elimination on consolidation.

- **Note 28 Company FY2025 comparative** [D005, physical PDF p. 67]: Dis-Chem Distribution purchases R16,197,272k vs FY2026 R18,728,461k (+15.6%) — faster than Group revenue growth of 9.3%. Verify whether this reflects a shift in intercompany pricing or mix.

        29. Financial risk management objectives and policies                     
           Financial assets                                                       
           Financial assets recognised on the statement of financial position include cash and cash equivalents, trade and other
           receivables and loans receivable. These financial assets are classified, at initial recognition, as subsequently measured at
           amortised cost.                                                        
           Initial recognition                                                    
           The classification of financial assets at initial recognition depends on the financial asset’s contractual cash flow characteristics
           and the Group’s business model for managing them. With the exception of trade receivables that do not contain a significant
           financing component or for which the Group has applied the practical expedient, the Group initially measures a financial
           asset at its fair value plus, in the case of a financial asset not at fair value through profit or loss, transaction costs. Trade
           receivables that do not contain a significant financing component or for which the Group has applied the practical expedient
           are measured at the transaction price under IFRS 15.                   
           The Group’s business model for managing financial assets refers to how it manages its financial assets in order to generate
           cash flows. The business model determines whether cash flows will result from collecting contractual cash flows, selling the
           financial assets, or both.                                             
           All regular way purchases and sales of financial assets are recognised on the trade date, which is the date that the Group
           commits to purchase the asset. Regular way purchases or sales are purchases or sales of financial assets that require delivery
           of assets within the period generally established by regulation or convention in the marketplace.
           Subsequent measurement                                                 
           Financial assets are subsequently classified as financial assets at amortised cost.
           Financial assets at amortised cost are subsequently measured using the effective interest (EIR) method and are subject to
           impairment. Gains and losses are recognised in profit or loss when the asset is derecognised, modified or impaired.
           Derecognition                                                          
           A financial asset (or, where applicable, a part of a financial asset or part of a group of similar financial assets) is primarily
           derecognised when:                                                     
           • The rights to receive cash flows from the asset have expired; or     
           • The Group has transferred its rights to receive cash flows from the asset or has assumed an obligation to pay the received
             cash flows in full without material delay to a third party under a “pass-through” arrangement; and either (a) the Group has
             transferred substantially all the risks and rewards of the asset, or (b) the Group has neither transferred nor retained
             substantially all the risks and rewards of the asset, but has transferred control of the asset.
           When the Group has transferred its rights to receive cash flows from an asset or has entered into a pass-through
           arrangement, it evaluates if, and to what extent, it has retained the risks and rewards of ownership. When it has neither
           transferred nor retained substantially all of the risks and rewards of the asset, nor transferred control of the asset, the Group
           continues to recognise the transferred asset to the extent of its continuing involvement. In that case, the Group also
           recognises an associated liability. The transferred asset and the associated liability are measured on a basis that reflects the
           rights and obligations that the Group has retained.                    
           Continuing involvement that takes the form of a guarantee over the transferred asset is measured at the lower of the original
           carrying amount of the asset and the maximum amount of consideration that the Group could be required to repay.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **"Various property companies" footnote** `[D005, physical PDF p. 68]`: "Relates to retail space that is owned/partially owned by certain directors." This qualifies the R128,676k lease liability and R(11,460)k interest expense to director-linked property entities. It confirms related-party property leases exist but does not state whether they are at market terms or whether they are included in the Group IFRS 16 lease liability of R2,943,233k. **Must verify in D006 (Note 22/28).**

- **"Related party receivable and payables are generally settled within 60 days"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 68]`: This is a qualification on the R861,985k loans receivable and R785,799k loans payable. "Generally" is a soft qualifier — it does not confirm all balances are current, nor does it address impairment. **Must verify ageing and ECL in D006 (Note 29).**

- **"Dividend received earned from subsidiaries, associates and joint ventures is disclosed in note 8"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 68]`: Cross-reference to Note 8; dividend income is not in this capture. **Must verify in D006 (Note 8).**

- **"Bonuses relate to amounts physically paid in the period"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 70]`: This qualifies the FY2025 bonus column (R7,340k executive, R8,030k prescribed officers). It means the bonus expense in the income statement may differ from cash paid due to accrual timing. **Must verify in D006 (Note 8/employee costs).**

- **"The employment contracts of executive directors differ from that of other employees in that they do not accrue leave and have a longer notice period"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 70]`: This qualifies the leave pay provision and termination liability. It means executive directors do not contribute to the leave pay accrual, reducing that liability relative to headcount. **Must verify in D006 (provisions note).**

- **"SE Saltzman resigned in the current financial year and therefore his remaining shares were forfeited"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 71]`: This confirms SE Saltzman's resignation and forfeiture of 34,315 (2023 offer) + 26,341 (2024 offer) = 60,656 shares. This is a governance event and affects the FSP expense reversal. **Must verify in D006 (Note 20 share-based payments).**

- **"In the current financial year, shares with offer date 31 August 2022 were exercised"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 71]`: Details on-market sales by directors/prescribed officers on 30 June 2025: JD Pope 14,667 for R475,654; SRN Goetsch 38,565 for R1,250,671; IL Saltzman 123,041 for R3,990,244; SE Saltzman 37,171 for R1,205,463; CJ Williams 51,420 for R1,667,561; LF Saltzman 100,840 for R3,270,261. Total 365,704 shares sold for ~R11,859,854. This is a **significant director share sale** and should be flagged for governance/confidence assessment. **Must verify in D006 (Note 19/20).**

- **"KS Sterling retired in the prior year and received 26,087 shares for offer date 31 August 2022 and 12,565 shares for offer date 31 August 2023"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 72]`: Prior-year qualification; confirms retirement treatment. Not material to FY2026 forecast.

- **"In the prior financial year JD Pope exercised 14,057 options at R478,581, TJ Ponter exercised 25,064 options at R853,930, Z Dindar exercised 25,064 options at R853,930 and R Govender exercised 3,884 options at R132,328"** `[D005, physical PDF p. 72]`: Prior-year SAR exercises; confirms SAR scheme is winding down (all 2019 options exercised or forfeited by FY2026). **Must verify in D006 (Note 20) whether any SAR liability remains.**

- **Note 29 financial risk management** `[D005, physical PDF p. 73]`: This is the start of the financial risk management note. It states financial assets are classified at amortised cost and subject to impairment under the EIR method. It does **not** yet disclose the credit risk, liquidity risk, or market risk sections — those must be in subsequent pages (physical pp. 74-77). **Must verify in D006 (Note 29 continuation) for ECL staging, satisfactory-paid %, collection rate, covenant headroom, and the R400m receivables pledge.**

           Impairment                                                             
           The Group recognises an allowance for expected credit losses (ECLs) for all debt instruments not held at fair value through
           profit or loss. ECLs are based on the difference between the contractual cash flows due in accordance with the contract and
           all the cash flows that the Group expects to receive. The carrying amount of the asset is reduced through use of an allowance
           account. The amount of the loss is recognised in profit or loss.       
           For trade receivables the Group applies a simplified approach using a provision matrix in calculating ECLs. An allowance for
           expected credit losses is made over the lifetime of a financial asset when the Group considers it to be in default (such as
           default or delinquency in payments, the probability of insolvency or significant financial difficulties of the debtor or group of
           debtors) that all of the amounts due under the original terms of the invoice/agreement will not be collected. Default occurs
           when a payment is 90 days past its due date. A financial asset is written off when there is no reasonable expectation of
           recovering the contractual cash flows.                                 
           For other receivables and loan receivables the Group applies the general approach in calculating ECLs. At each reporting
           date, the Group recognises a loss allowance based on either 12-month ECLs or lifetime ECLs, depending on whether there
           has been a significant increase in credit risk on the financial instrument since initial recognition.
           Financial liabilities                                                  
           Financial liabilities recognised on the statement of financial position include bank overdraft, trade and other payables and
           loans payable. These financial liabilities are classified, at initial recognition, as financial liabilities at fair value through profit or
           loss or financial liabilities at amortised cost, as appropriate.       
           Initial recognition                                                    
           All financial liabilities are recognised initially at fair value and, in the case of financial liabilities at amortised cost, net of
           directly attributable transaction costs.                               
           Subsequent measurement                                                 
           The measurement of financial liabilities depends on their classification, as described below:
           Financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss:            
           Financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss include financial liabilities held for trading and financial liabilities
           designated upon initial recognition as at fair value through profit or loss. Financial liabilities are classified as held for trading if
           they are incurred for the purpose of repurchasing in the near term.    
           Gains or losses on liabilities held for trading are recognised in profit or loss.
           Financial liabilities at amortised cost:                               
           After initial recognition, interest-bearing financial liabilities at amortised cost are subsequently measured at amortised cost
           using the EIR method. Gains and losses are recognised in profit or loss when the liabilities are derecognised as well as
           through the EIR amortisation process.                                  
           Amortised cost is calculated by taking into account any discount or premium on acquisition and fees or costs that are an
           integral part of the EIR. The EIR amortisation is included as finance costs in the statement of comprehensive income.
           Derecognition                                                          
           A financial liability is derecognised when the obligation under the liability is discharged or cancelled or expires. When an
           existing financial liability is replaced by another from the same lender on substantially different terms, or the terms of an
           existing liability are substantially modified, such an exchange or modification is treated as the derecognition of the original
           liability and the recognition of a new liability. The difference in the respective carrying amounts is recognised in profit or loss.
           Offsetting of financial instruments                                    
           Financial assets and financial liabilities are offset and the net amount is reported in the statement of financial position if, and
           only if, there is a currently enforceable legal right to offset the recognised amounts and there is an intention to settle on a net
           basis, to realise the assets and settle the liabilities simultaneously.

           Fair value measurement                                                 
           In addition to the financial instruments carried at fair value (FVTPL), the fair values of financial instruments measured at
           amortised cost are disclosed should it be determined that the carrying value of these instruments does not reasonably
           approximate their fair value at each reporting date. Fair value is the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to
           transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date.
           The fair value measurement is based on the presumption that the transaction to sell the asset or transfer the liability takes
           place either:                                                          
           • In the principal market for the asset or liability; or               
           • In the absence of a principal market, in the most advantageous market for the asset or liability.
           The principal or the most advantageous market must be accessible by the Group.
           The fair value of an asset or a liability is measured using the assumptions that market participants would use when pricing the
           asset or liability, assuming that market participants act in their economic best interest.
           A fair value measurement of a non-financial asset takes into account a market participant’s ability to generate economic
           benefits by using the asset in its highest and best use or by selling it to another market participant that would use the asset in
           its highest and best use.                                              
           The valuation techniques that are used to measure fair value are appropriate in the circumstances and for which sufficient
           data is available, maximising the use of relevant observable inputs and minimising the use of unobservable inputs.
           All assets and liabilities for which fair value is measured or disclosed in the financial statements are categorised within the fair
           value hierarchy, described as follows, based on the lowest level input that is significant to the fair value measurement as a
           whole:                                                                 
           • Level 1: Quoted (unadjusted) market prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.
           • Level 2: Valuation techniques for which the lowest level input that is significant to the fair value measurement is directly or
             indirectly observable.                                               
           • Level 3: Valuation techniques for which the lowest level input that is significant to the fair value measurement is
             unobservable.                                                        
           For assets and liabilities that are recognised in the financial statements at fair value, or for which the fair value is disclosed, on
           a recurring basis, it is determined whether transfers have occurred between the levels in the hierarchy by re-assessing
           categorisation (based on the lowest level input that is significant to the fair value measurement as a whole) at the end of each
           reporting period.
