           Credit risk                                                            
           The carrying amount of financial assets represents the maximum credit exposure which relates to trade and other receivables,
           loans receivables and positive cash and cash equivalents.              
           Trade and other receivables                                            
           The Group is exposed to credit risk in relation to trade and other receivables from its retail and wholesale business.
                                                           2026     2025          
                                                           R’000    R’000         
           The maximum exposure to credit risk for trade receivables is as follows:
           Retail                                        485 680   390 192        
           Wholesale                                    1 389 819 1 193 829       
           The maximum exposure to credit risk for other receivables and accrued income
           is as follows:                                                         
           Retail                                       1 107 432 1 026 999       
           Wholesale                                     611 877   479 218        
           In relation to the retail business, trade receivables primarily relate to amounts recoverable from medical aids. These
           receivables are deemed to be low credit risk as medical schemes pay mainly within 14 days and amounts are neither past
           due nor impaired.                                                      
           The majority of other receivables and accrued income in retail and wholesale relate to rebates, promotions and advertising
           and logistic fee receivables from suppliers and are deemed to be low credit risk as the net position with the supplier is a
           creditor. Other receivables are currently measured in Stage 1 based on 12-month ECL's.
           In wholesale, customers are primarily independent pharmacies and other pharmaceutical companies. The risk is managed
           through formal procedures for granting of credit to trade debtors. Credit quality of underlying wholesale customers is
           assessed before credit is granted and re-assessed on a regular basis. The Group determines the allowance for expected
           credit loss by means of applying a percentage that reflects the best estimate of expected credit losses at the reporting date
           determined with reference to past history to the relevant age buckets of the trade debtors adjusted for forward-looking
           information (i.e. current and future pharmaceutical market and legislation as it relates to Single Exit Price (SEP) pricing). The
           process for managing wholesale credit risk is to allow 10 days after payment is due, for customers to pay. If payment is not
           subsequently made after following up with the customer, the customer’s account will be suspended until payment is received
           or a payment plan is implemented.                                      
           Cash and cash equivalents                                              
           With respect to the credit risk arising from cash resources, the Group’s exposure to credit risk arises from the default of the
           counterparty with the maximum exposure equal to the carrying amount of these resources.
           The Group manages and monitors daily funding requirements and has limited foreign currency exposure. Surplus funds are
           invested with banking institutions of a high credit standing.          
           Loans receivable                                                       
           The Group is exposed to credit risk in relation to loans with related and other parties. The risk is managed through formal
           procedures for granting of the loans and the recoverability thereof is assessed annually.
           NCI shareholders loans                                                 
           NCI shareholder loans are full recourse loans that are receivable from individuals that have non-controlling interests in
           subsidiary companies of the Group. The dividends they receive from the subsidiary companies must, in accordance with the
           loan agreement, be used to repay the loans and therefore based on the expected profitability and dividend policy there is no
           expectation that the loans will not be recovered. These loans are unsecured and non-interest bearing.
           Related party loans                                                    
           Related party loans consist of loans to associates/ joint ventures of the Group (BEESECDP, Tony Ferguson, Sable and Dis-
           Chem Life (2025: including Nexus)). No security is held for these loans and they are repayable on demand.
           These entities are in a forecasted profitable position and therefore deemed to be a low credit risk. The Tony Ferguson loan
           earns interest at prime, Sable at prime plus 0.5%, Nexus at prime, Dis-Chem Life at the average bank overdraft rate and the
           BEESECDCP loan does not earn interest. The Nexus loan was repaid in the current financial year.
           TLC loans                                                              
           TLC loans relate to loans given to TLC franchise stores and earn interest linked to prime. They are secured by the inventory
           held in the store and the operating licence. The companies are in a profitable position and have sufficient liquid assets in
           order to repay the loans and therefore deemed to be a low credit risk.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`, note references) appear in the supplied pp. 74–77 evidence.** No missing-footnote issue arises for this capture.
- **Default definition (p. 74)**: Default occurs when a payment is 90 days past due; write-off when no reasonable expectation of recovering contractual cash flows. This is the trigger for Stage 3 classification and must be reconciled to the Note 29 ECL staging (Q-3e72d5f6 / Q-6a037c6d).
- **Simplified vs general approach (p. 74)**: Trade receivables use a provision matrix (lifetime ECL); other receivables and loan receivables use the general approach (12-month or lifetime ECL depending on significant increase in credit risk). This determines where the R3,605,507k trade and other receivables and R195,670k loans receivable are provisioned — verify the split in Note 17/29.
- **Retail trade receivables qualification (p. 77)**: "deemed to be low credit risk as medical schemes pay mainly within 14 days and amounts are neither past due nor impaired" — a management assertion, not a quantified ageing. Must be tested against the Note 29 ageing and satisfactory-paid %.
- **Other receivables/rebates qualification (p. 77)**: "deemed to be low credit risk as the net position with the supplier is a creditor" and "currently measured in Stage 1 based on 12-month ECLs." This is a netting-based credit argument; it does not address gross recoverability of the R1,107,432k retail and R611,877k wholesale other/accrued receivables if supplier relationships terminate. Verify against Note 17 ageing (Q-ae621d5e).
- **Wholesale credit process (p. 77)**: 10-day grace after due date, then suspension or payment plan; ECL percentage applied to age buckets adjusted for forward-looking SEP pricing/legislation. Verify the forward-looking overlay and payment-plan population in Note 29.
- **NCI shareholder loans (p. 77)**: Full recourse, unsecured, non-interest bearing, repaid from dividends; "no expectation that the loans will not be recovered." Verify against Note 18/29 balances and any ECL.
- **Related-party loans (p. 77)**: BEESECDP, Tony Ferguson, Sable and Dis-Chem Life (2025: including Nexus); unsecured, repayable on demand; interest at prime (Tony Ferguson), prime + 0.5% (Sable), average bank overdraft rate (Dis-Chem Life), nil (BEESECDP); Nexus repaid in the current year. This partially answers Q-d58da8bb/Q-4dddc203 but does not quantify balances or impairment.
- **TLC loans (p. 77)**: Prime-linked, secured by store inventory and operating licence; "profitable position and sufficient liquid assets" — assertion only; verify against Note 18 balance (R43,029k per stored ledger) and impairment (Q-7af40670).
- **Fair value hierarchy (p. 75)**: Level 1/2/3 definitions given; no Level 3 sensitivity or transfers disclosed in this capture. Verify in the fair-value note.
- **Financial liability derecognition/modification (p. 74)**: Substantial-modification accounting could affect the R2,027,578k loans payable if refinanced — relevant to the Standard Bank bullet facility maturing 31 May 2027 (Q-a3270ab2).

           Currency risk                                                          
           The Group's exposure to the risk of changes in foreign exchange rates relates primarily to the supply chain finance
           programme and import vendors. As part of the process of managing the Group's currency risk, foreign exchange contracts
           (FEC) may be taken out if deemed necessary.                            
           A FEC liability of R3.7 million (2025: Rnil) is recognised at 28 February 2026. As at 28 February 2026 the Group had foreign
           balances of USD11.9 million (R189 million), EUR2.6 million (R50 million) and GBP0.02 million (R0.5 million). As at 28
           February 2025 the Group had foreign balances of USD14.3 million (R261 million), EUR2.4 million (R47 million) and GBP0.1
           million (R3.2 million).                                                
           If the exchange rate, with all other variables held constant, increased or decreased by R2.00 (2025: R2.00) at year-end, the
           impact of the Group’s profit before tax would be approximately R33.4 million (2025: R33.7 million).
           Interest rate risk                                                     
           The Group's exposure to the risk of changes in market interest rates relates primarily to the Absa and Standard Bank loans
           with floating interest rates linked to JIBAR as well as interest incurred on overdraft facilities (note 9).
           As part of the process of managing the Group’s interest rate risk, interest rate characteristics of new borrowings and
           refinancing of existing borrowings are positioned according to anticipated movements in interest rates. Funds on call earn
           interest at prevailing market call rates. Interest payable on bank borrowings fluctuates in accordance with prime bank lending
           rates while the Absa, Standard Bank, FNB and Investec loans fluctuate with the JIBAR and prime rate and the Supply Chain
           Financing with the SONIA or similar reference rate. The South African Reserve Bank has confirmed that JIBAR will cease on 31
           December 2026, after which South Africa will transition to alternative reference rates. JIBAR is expected to be replaced by
           ZARONIA, a near risk free rate administered under the oversight of the South African Reserve Bank. Any margin adjustments
           required as part of the transition will be calibrated to replicate the equivalent JIBAR based pricing, such that there is no
           material impact on the overall interest rates agreed. The majority of the loan agreements already provide for the JIBAR rates
           to transition to ZARONIA, the remaining loan agreements will be amended before JIBAR ceases on 31 December 2026.
           If the interest rate, with all other variables held constant, increased or decreased by 200 average basis points (2025: 200) at
           year-end, the impact of the Group’s profit before tax would be approximately R58 million (2025: R59 million). The sensitivity
           analysis for both periods presented was based on the average balance of the funds during the period on the bank
           borrowings, Absa loan, Standard Bank loan, FNB loan, Supply Chain Finance, Investec loan and other loans.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`) appear on pp. 78–81.** The qualifications are embedded in narrative text and table notes:
  - **"The majority of the loan agreements already provide for the JIBAR rates to transition to ZARONIA, the remaining loan agreements will be amended before JIBAR ceases on 31 December 2026."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 78]` — This is a forward-looking qualification. It implies a minority of loan agreements still lack fallback language. The "no material impact" assertion rests on margin calibration replicating JIBAR pricing; this must be verified against actual facility terms in Note 23 (D006). If calibration is not exact, FY2027 finance costs could step up.
  - **"Any margin adjustments required as part of the transition will be calibrated to replicate the equivalent JIBAR based pricing, such that there is no material impact on the overall interest rates agreed."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 78]` — Management assertion, not evidenced by a build-up. Needs verification.
  - **"Dis-Chem has sufficient head room in both these ratios and does not expect these ratios to be defaulted on in the next 12 months."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 79]` — Qualitative only; no quantified headroom. The gearing ratio of 2.6x (2025: 2.3x) is disclosed but the covenant thresholds are not. This is a material gap for going-concern assessment.
  - **"There are no covenants in place for Investec or Supply Chain Finance."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 79]` — Reduces covenant risk on those facilities but also means no lender-imposed discipline; the SCF R1.7bn facility is uncommitted from a covenant perspective.
  - **"There were no material business combinations or foreign exchange differences or other non-cash transfers relating to the carrying amount of liabilities subject to this supply chain finance arrangement."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 79]` — Confirms SCF payables are pure cash-flow driven; no non-cash inflation of the R965m balance.
  - **"Trade receivables primarily relate to amounts recoverable from medical aids. These receivables are deemed to be low credit risk as medical schemes pay mainly within 14 days and amounts are neither past due nor impaired."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 81]` — Company-level assertion. No ageing table supplied to test it. If medical scheme payment behaviour has deteriorated (consistent with the "constrained consumer" narrative), this assertion could be stale.
  - **"The majority of other receivables and accrued income relates to rebates, promotions and advertising receivable from suppliers and are deemed to be low credit risk as the net position with the supplier is a creditor. Other receivables are currently measured in Stage 1 based on 12-month ECLs."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 81]` — The netting argument is a qualification: if supplier relationships terminate or rebate disputes arise, the "creditor net position" offset disappears and these receivables become exposed. All Stage 1 means no lifetime ECL recognised — potentially under-provisioned if supplier stress emerges.
  - **"The majority of the loans receivable are companies within the Dis-Chem Group and based on budgets prepared and current profitability will be able to repay the loans and therefore deemed to be a low credit risk."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 81]` — Company-level; these are eliminated on consolidation. The residual external loans (Uphawu, The Tailor) are expected repaid within 12 months but no ECL is raised.
  - **"Other loans mainly relate to the loans given to Uphawu and The Tailor, companies in the cut and trim industry, which is expected to be repaid within the next 12 months."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 81]` — No impairment assessment disclosed for these external loans.
  - **"A FEC liability of R3.7 million (2025: Rnil) is recognised at 28 February 2026."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 78]` — New FX derivative liability; small but signals hedging activity resumed.
  - **"If the exchange rate... increased or decreased by R2.00... impact... approximately R33.4 million (2025: R33.7 million)."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 78]` — FX sensitivity is material relative to PBT; must be modelled.
  - **"If the interest rate... increased or decreased by 200 average basis points... impact... approximately R58 million (2025: R59 million)."** `[D005, physical PDF p. 78]` — Interest rate sensitivity; implies average net floating debt of ~R2.9bn.

           Interest rate risk                                                     
           The company’s exposure to the risk of changes in market interest rates relates primarily to the Absa loan with a floating
           interest rate linked to JIBAR as well as interest incurred on overdraft facilities (note 9).
           As part of the process of managing the company’s interest rate risk, interest rate characteristics of new borrowings and
           refinancing of existing borrowings are positioned according to anticipated movements in interest rates. Funds on call earn
           interest at prevailing market call rates. Interest payable on bank borrowings and the Investec loan fluctuate in accordance
           with prime bank lending rates while the Absa loans fluctuate with the JIBAR rate.
           If the interest rate, with all other variables held constant, increased or decreased by 200 average basis points at year-end
           (2025: 200), the impact of the company’s profit before tax would be approximately R46 million (2025: R33 million). The
           sensitivity analysis presented was based on the average balance of the funds during the period on the bank borrowings and
           Absa loan.

           (2025: R786 million).                                                  
           Dis-Chem Pharmacies have given security/guarantees to ABSA, Standard Bank and Nedbank in regard to certain companies
           within the Dis-Chem Group and landlords. Securities/guarantees to ABSA for R2.2 billion in regard to Dis-Chem Distribution;
           to Bemax International (R75 million), Dis-Chem Distribution (R440 million) and CJ Pharmaceutical (R400 million); and to
           Nedbank for R2 million in regard to landlords. These facilities have not been used at year end. Included in guarantees is an
           unrestricted cession of loans receivable and cash management accounts to Standard Bank. This has not been called upon.
           The debt covenants for the ABSA loan (which is tested at February and August) is based on interest cover ratio
           (EBITDA/finance charges) and net leverage (ratio of total net debt to EBITDA). Dis-Chem has sufficient head room in both
           these ratios and does not expect these ratios to be met in the next 12 months. There are no covenants in place for Investec.
           The board believes that the debt levels of the company are acceptable with a gearing ratio (excluding finance leases) of 2.3
           (2025: 2.5).

30. Capital management
The primary objective of the Group’s and company's capital management is to ensure that it maintains a strong credit rating
and healthy capital ratios in order to support its business and maximise shareholder value. This was met in the current and
prior year.
The Group and company considers share capital and retained income as capital. The board of directors considers capital
requirements from time to time and makes adjustments accordingly.
No changes were made in the objectives, policies and processes for managing capital during the years ended
28 February 2026 and 28 February 2025.
31. Events after the reporting period
The Group has been impacted by fluctuations in exchange rates and fuel prices after the reporting period but this has not
had a material impact on the Group and continues to be assessed.
The Group took out an additional bullet loan of R500 million with a maturity date of two years (which can be extended to
three years) and earns interest at the three-month JIBAR plus 1.3%. S189 restructuring focused on specific head office and
administrative roles to realign the business's operating model, but simultaneously creating 200 new roles in underinvested
departments.
The Group and company have no other significant events after the reporting period.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers** (`[^1]`, `*`, etc.) appear in the supplied pages 82–85. No missing-footnote issue arises here.
- **Covenant wording anomaly** `[D005, p. 82]`: "does not expect these ratios to be met in the next 12 months" — as printed, this reads as a covenant breach expectation, contradicting "sufficient head room". Likely a drafting error ("breached"), but must be verified against the covenant note in D006. Material for going-concern and forecast.
- **"These facilities have not been used at year end"** `[D005, p. 82]`: refers to the ABSA/Standard Bank/Nedbank guarantees and the R400m CJ Pharmaceutical guarantee. Yet the maturity table shows bank overdraft R1,666,720k drawn — so the "unused" statement must refer to the guarantee/security lines, not the working capital facilities. Needs reconciliation.
- **Gearing 2.3 (2025: 2.5)** `[D005, p. 82]`: "excluding finance leases" — definition of numerator/denominator not stated; cannot be reconciled to reported net debt without the covenant note.
- **Interest rate sensitivity R46m (2025: R33m)** `[D005, p. 82]`: based on average balance of funds during the period, not year-end balance — so it understates/overstates year-end exposure depending on intra-year debt path. Note the 39% YoY increase in sensitivity vs the modest increase in facilities.
- **Note 31 S189 restructuring** `[D005, p. 83]`: no rand cost, no headcount reduction number, no timing disclosed. This is a potential FY2027 one-off restructuring charge and/or employee cost saving — must be quantified in D006 (employee costs / other expenses).
- **Note 31 new R500m bullet at 3M JIBAR + 1.3%** `[D005, p. 83]`: post-year-end, so not in FY2026 finance costs. Adds ~R500m × (JIBAR+1.3%) to FY2027 finance costs — needs JIBAR assumption. Also increases net debt and leverage covenant headroom pressure.
- **Note 31 FX/fuel** `[D005, p. 83]`: "not had a material impact … continues to be assessed" — unquantified; relevant to FY2027 gross margin (imported goods, freight).
- **Shareholder analysis** `[D005, pp. 84–85]`: total issued 860,084,483; treasury 3,974,878; net 856,109,605. Beneficial >3% total 69.39%; fund managers >3% total 47.03%. Coronation fund-manager holding 26.80% vs beneficial 14.88% — the gap reflects nominee/stockbroker holdings; not an error but worth noting for free-float analysis.

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`, note refs) are present** in the supplied p. 5 evidence. There is therefore no footnote text to unpack or to flag as missing from this capture.
- **Embedded column-header commentary (material):** The income statement table carries a dual-basis presentation — a headline `% change` column and a second `% change` column headed (decoded) *"excluding non-recurring items and ecosystem expenses and property gain"* `[D001, physical PDF p. 5]`. This is a **management-adjusted (non-IFRS) growth basis** presented alongside statutory growth. It changes the read of every line: e.g. operating profit statutory −11.9% vs adjusted +18.2%; headline earnings statutory −17.1% vs adjusted +19.3%. Any forecast built on the adjusted column must strip out the excluded items (ecosystem expenses, property gain, non-recurring items) and confirm their rand amounts in D002/D005 — they are **not quantified on this page**.

Its nature (new-format store/Health Hub rollout, digital/platform investment, or one-off) is critical to whether the adjusted margin is sustainable. Flagged as a verification question (Q-new-2).
- **Property gain:** A property gain is excluded from the adjusted basis, implying a one-off property disposal gain sits in FY2026 statutory operating profit. Amount not shown here; must be located in D002/D005 (Q-new-3).

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`, note references) are present on physical p. 6.** There is therefore no footnote text to unpack or to flag as missing from this capture. This is itself a verification point: the revenue and total-income tables carry no printed qualifications, so any adjustment (property gain, ecosystem expenses, intergroup elimination basis) must be sought on adjacent pages (p. 5 and pp. 7-24).
- **Embedded qualification — "excluding property gain"**: The total-income table presents a second "% change" and "% margin" column explicitly *excluding property gain* (FY2026 30.7% vs FY2025 30.7%). This is a management-adjusted basis, not a statutory one. It implies a property gain is embedded in FY2026 total income (and possibly FY2025) that management considers non-recurring. The rand amount of that gain is **not printed on this page** — it must be quantified on p. 5 or in the notes (Note 8 / PPE disposal note). Until quantified, the 30.9% headline margin overstates the recurring margin by an unknown amount.
- **Embedded qualification — "excluding the property gain" in the store-sales total-income bullet**: The bullet states store-sales total income declined 8.1% *including* the property gain but rose 0% *excluding* it (R2,699m vs R2,696m). This is a material qualification: the headline -8.1% is flattered/distorted by a property gain sitting in the prior or current year base. The exact gain amount and which year it falls in must be verified.
- **Intergroup elimination basis**: Intergroup revenue R(1,814)m and intergroup total income R(739)m are shown as separate elimination lines. The intergroup total-income elimination (R739m) is large relative to total income (R13,216m) — ~5.6% — and its growth (+12.3%) outpaces group revenue growth (+9.3%). The basis of intergroup margin (i.e., whether intergroup sales carry a different margin than external sales) is not explained here and should be checked in the segmental note.
- **"Total income" vs "revenue" definition**: The page uses "total income" (R13,216m) which is larger than "total group revenue" (R42,826m) only as a margin concept — total income margin 30.9%. The composition of total income (gross profit + other income + customer financial services revenue?) is not defined on this page and must be confirmed against the income statement (D002) and Note 7.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section

No stored questions can be resolved from this section. The evidence on physical p. 7 contains only retail and wholesale operating expenditure tables (with CID-encoded glyphs) and no data on revenue, credit book, store portfolio, auditor's report, or primary statements. All stored questions are carried forward in Section 4.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers or definitions are present** in the supplied evidence `[D001, physical PDF p. 7]`. The tables carry no `[^1]`, `*`, or note references. No qualification text is printed.
- **CID-encoded glyphs**: All line-item labels and figures are rendered as CID codes (e.g., `(cid:24)(cid:286)(cid:393)(cid:396)(cid:286)(cid:272)(cid:349)(cid:258)(cid:410)(cid:349)(cid:381)(cid:374)` = "Depreciation and amortisation"). Decoding is possible for the numeric figures but the labels require verification against a plain-text capture. This is an encoding artefact, not a financial qualification.
- **Decoded figures (provisional, pending plain-text confirmation)**:
  - Retail: Depreciation & amortisation (1,150) vs (1,001), +14.9%; Occupancy costs (633) vs (636), -0.5%; Employment costs (3,221) vs (2,895), +11.3%; Other operating costs (2,869) vs (2,271), +26.3%; Total retail costs (7,873) vs (6,803), +15.7%.
  - Retail store metrics: Revenue growth 9.3%, Payroll cost growth 7.9%, Difference 1.4%, Number of stores 268.
  - Wholesale: Depreciation & amortisation (193) vs (188), -2.6%; Occupancy costs (68) vs (62), +9.7%; Employment costs (800) vs (722), +10.8%; Other operating costs (1,120) vs (1,112), +0.7%; Total wholesale costs (2,181) vs (2,084), +4.7%.
- **Arithmetic check**: Retail total (7,873) = 1,150+633+3,221+2,869 = 7,873 ✓. Wholesale total (2,181) = 193+68+800+1,120 = 2,181 ✓. No reconciliation discrepancy in the totals.
- **Material observation**: Retail "Other operating costs" grew +26.3% vs revenue +9.3% — a 17pp gap that is the single largest driver of the +15.7% total retail cost growth. This is not explained by any footnote in this capture and must be verified (see Q-new below). Wholesale "Other operating costs" is essentially flat (+0.7%) despite revenue growth, which is a notable divergence from retail.

### [ANALYST QUERY / EMPHASIS]
Scrutinize key accounting policies, unusual movements, and forward guidance. This is one capture, not proof of whole-report coverage. Adjacent tables/footnotes may need verification.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section
No stored questions can be resolved from this capture. The evidence on physical pp. 8–9 is CID-glyph-encoded and contains no legible footnote definitions, no credit-book metrics, no store portfolio table, and no primary-statement figures. All stored questions remain open and are carried forward in Section 4.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive
- Physical p. 9 contains footnote markers `[^13]` (against the FY2025 Working capital Days column) and `[^14]` (against the Working capital management heading). **Neither footnote definition is present in this capture** — the text is missing, not merely illegible. A verification question is raised (Section 3, Q1).
- The Working capital Days table (p. 9) shows FY2026 vs FY2025: Debtor days 30 vs 28; Inventory days 86 vs 91; Creditor days 92 vs 98; **Total working capital 28 vs 29**. Arithmetic check: 30 + 86 − 92 = 24, not 28; 28 + 91 − 98 = 21, not 29. The printed "Total working capital" does not equal the sum of the three components on either year — a reconciliation discrepancy requiring the footnote definition (Q1).
- The Inventory days vs Creditor days chart (p. 9) is a multi-year series (FY2018–FY2026) with overlapping data labels; the FY2026 inventory-days label appears as 77 and creditor-days as 79, which conflicts with the table's 86 and 92. This is a chart-vs-table tension to verify (Q2).
- Physical p. 8 operating-profit table (decoded): Retail R1,866m vs R1,956m (−6.9%); Wholesale R362m vs R519m (−30.7%); Intergroup R29m vs R9m (+191.2%); **Total group R1,857m vs R2,108m (−11.9%)**, margin 5.8% vs 8.7%. Arithmetic check: 1,866 + 362 + 29 = 2,257, not 1,857 — a R400m gap; the "Total group" line does not foot from the three segments. This is a material reconciliation discrepancy (Q3).
- EPS/HEPS table (p. 8): Basic EPS 118.6c vs 137.6c (−13.8%); Basic HEPS 113.7c vs 137.9c (−17.7%); Diluted EPS 119.4c vs 137.8c; Diluted HEPS 114.2c vs 138.1c. Note the bullet states HEPS decreased 17.7% (consistent with 113.7 vs 137.9), while the stored ledger references a −17.1% HEPS figure — a discrepancy to reconcile (Q4).
- The p. 8 bullet "Operating expenses increased by 18.0% and 19.3%, respectively" is ambiguous (which two measures?) and is not footnoted; the operating-profit table shows total group operating profit *declining* 11.9%, so the 18–19% expense growth must be reconciled to the margin bridge (Q5).

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Physical p. 10 — Cash management bridge (CID-encoded):** The visible numeric fragments `3124`, `97`, `(512)`, `(403)`, `(523)`, `(1 089)`, `(139)`, `(984)`, `(429)` appear to be a cash-flow waterfall (likely opening cash → operating cash → capex → dividends → financing → closing cash). The axis labels are CID-encoded and cannot be read reliably. **No footnote markers are visible on this page.** The bridge cannot be reconciled to the stored ledger's cash-flow figures (OCF, FCF, net debt) without a plain-text re-capture. This is a material gap because the stored ledger has multiple open questions on OCF/FCF/net-debt reconciliation (Q-8f31c9dde0434bc2, Q-a0e1efc9e2fb465b, Q-4497778bcc6a42f2).
- **Physical p. 10 — Capital management table:** Legible structure: `R'm | FY2026 | FY2025 | % change` with three rows (expansion capex, maintenance capex, total capex) and a `%` block (expansion capex to turnover, maintenance capex to turnover, total capex to turnover). The numeric cells are CID-encoded and cannot be transcribed. **No footnote markers visible.** The `%` block implies capex-to-turnover ratios are a management KPI — this is a forecast input that must be re-captured in plain text.
- **Physical p. 11 — Core category market shares table:** Legible structure: `Market share (%) | FY2026¹ | FY2025#` with three rows (dispensary, front shop and beauty, baby care). Footnote markers `¹` and `#` are present but **their definitions are not in the supplied evidence** — the footnote text is missing from this capture. The `#` on FY2025 and `¹` on FY2026 suggest a restatement or definitional change in the comparative, which is material for market-share trend analysis. A verification question is raised (Section 3).
- **Physical p. 11 — Bullet commentary (CID-encoded):** Four bullets are visible but only partially decodable. The fourth bullet appears to reference "Baby Care at 18.0%" and "including Baby City" — suggesting the market-share table's baby-care figure may include the acquired Baby City business, which would make the FY2026 vs FY2025 comparison non-like-for-like. This must be verified against the footnote definitions.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive
- **No footnote markers or footnote definitions are present on p. 13.** The table has no `[^1]`/`*` markers and no printed note block. Therefore no footnote text is missing from this capture — there is simply none on this page. This does not confirm absence elsewhere in the deck.
- **Table structure qualification (critical):** The table is a three-block layout — `Retail` (FY2026, FY2025, % change), `Investment in ecosystem and non-recurring expenses` (FY2026 only, no comparative), and `Core retail` (FY2026, FY2025, % change). The "Core retail" column is an **adjusted** measure that adds back the ecosystem/non-recurring column to Retail. This is a management-adjusted basis, not a statutory line, and the add-back is not footnoted or defined on this page. It must be reconciled to the income statement and Note 8.

| Expenses | (9,628) | (8,573) | 12.3 | 492 | (9,136) | (8,573) | 6.6 |

- **Arithmetic checks on the decoded table:**
  - Retail total income margin: 11,390/36,596 = **31.1%**; FY2025 10,159/33,584 = **30.2%** → +0.9pp. Consistent with the p. 12 "+0.9%" total income margin change (resolves part of Q-7bc3b4f051b24de2 on definition: it is percentage points, retail scope).
  - Core retail total income margin: 11,390/36,578 = **31.1%**; FY2025 30.2% → +0.9pp.
  - Retail operating margin: 1,762/36,596 = **4.8%**; FY2025 1,586/33,584 = **4.7%**. But the printed operating profit % change is **(6.9)%** while revenue grew 9.0% — this is internally inconsistent: 1,762 vs 1,586 is **+11.1%**, not (6.9)%. **Flag as a decoding/arithmetic discrepancy** (see Q-new below).
  - Core retail operating profit 1,857 vs 1,762 + 492 = 2,254 — does **not** reconcile (difference 397). The add-back column (492) exceeds the operating-profit uplift (95). **Flag.**
  - Core retail profit 1,519 vs 1,367 + 492 = 1,859 — does **not** reconcile. **Flag.**
  - Retail profit % change printed (11.9)% but 1,367 vs 1,216 = **+12.4%**. Sign/decode discrepancy. **Flag.**
  - Core retail profit % change printed 25.2% but 1,519 vs 1,216 = **+24.9%** (close; rounding).
- **Bullet call-outs (decoded):**
  - "Core retail profit before tax (excluding the R998m investment in the ecosystem) increased by 26.1%" — note this says **R998m**, whereas the table's ecosystem/non-recurring column totals 18 + 0 + 492 = **R510m**. **Material inconsistency (R998m vs R510m)** — flag.
  - "56% (R330m) invested in establishing and operationalising a biller lab and Dis-Chem Life" — R330m is 33% of R998m, not 56%. **Flag.**
  - "24% (R115m) relates to the non-recurring expenses to retire the benefit points programme and launch Better World's" — R115m is 11.5% of R998m, not 24%. **Flag.**
  - The three bullets (56% + 24% = 80%) leave 20% (~R200m) unexplained against R998m.
- **"X, bigly labs: Powering Dis-Chem's next growth horizon"** call-out lists six integration pillars (Digital Engagement, Loyalty Programme, Customer-Centric Personalisation, Integrated Healthcare, Embedded Value-Added Services, Modernised Store Network) — forward-looking, no rand amounts, no timeline. Treat as qualitative guidance only.

### [ANALYST QUERY / EMPHASIS]
Scrutinize key accounting policies, unusual movements, and forward guidance. This is one capture, not proof of whole-report coverage. Adjacent tables/footnotes may need verification.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Stored Questions Answered by This Section

No stored questions can be resolved or materially advanced by pages 15–16. The captured material is a Better Rewards programme performance appendix (sales uplift, volume share, basket metrics, discount cost). It does not contain the income statement, credit book, store portfolio, lease, tax, or note-level disclosures that the stored ledger questions target. All stored questions are carried forward unchanged in Section 4.

One partial data point is relevant to the loyalty questions (Q-b6e3cd4411864794, Q-9fab8087ee9545e3, Q-b643099191f5418f): the deck confirms Better Rewards is a live, discount-funded programme with quantified discount value returned to customers (Section 5), which is consistent with the loyalty liability collapse and points-issuance decline flagged earlier. This is corroborative only, not a resolution.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **No footnote markers or footnote definitions are present on either captured page.** Both pages are chart/table slides with bullet commentary; there is no `[^n]`, `*`, or note block. No missing-footnote question is raised for these pages.
- **CID-encoded glyphs**: nearly all numeric and text content on pp. 15–16 is rendered as `(cid:xxxx)` glyphs. Decoded values are reconstructed from the CID mapping and must be treated as unverified until a plain-text re-capture. This is an encoding artefact, not a report qualification.
- **Period qualification (p. 15)**: the sales table compares two non-annual windows — "01 March 2025 to 20 October 2025" vs "21 October 2025 to 19 May 2026". These are ~34-week and ~30-week periods respectively, not equal-length periods and not full financial years. Any growth read-across to FY2026 revenue is therefore invalid without normalisation. This is the single most consequential qualification in the capture.
- **"Since launch" basis (p. 16)**: the R1,126.9m total discount value and its boost-type split are cumulative since programme launch, not FY2026-only. They cannot be used as an annual P&L cost without a launch date and a period split.
- **"Total Income Margin" (p. 15)**: 30.8% vs 31.6% is presented as a Better Rewards cohort metric; it is not reconciled to the group total-income margin of 30.9% cited on p. 6. Scope (cohort vs group) is unconfirmed.
- **"Volume Share Gain" (p. 26 chart)**: the chart shows share gain by competitor/retailer category with no stated base, period, or source. It is a directional claim, not a reconcilable metric.

  - "Customer shift in how healthcare is delivered across all dimensions of retailing, from store design to product assortment, technology and process flow" — implies opex/capex and assortment change; unquantified `[D001, physical PDF p. 17]`.

No footnote or qualification explains the deterioration.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section
No stored questions can be resolved or partially answered from the material in this section (p. 19–20). The content is limited to store rollout tables, a property/lease strategy note, and an organisational chart; it contains no financial statements, credit metrics, or accounting-policy disclosures. All stored questions are carried forward in Section 4.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive
- **No footnote markers or definitions** appear on physical pp. 19–20. The only qualifications are two bullet points on p. 19:
  - "Committed stores and pipeline at 167 000m²" `[D001, physical PDF p. 19]` — this is a forward commitment/pipeline figure, not a signed-lease or capex commitment. It must be verified against Note 22 lease additions and the store-portfolio table in later sections.
  - "Double store opening rate since FY2023 driven by structured property methodology" `[D001, physical PDF p. 19]` — a management claim with no quantified base; the FY2023 opening rate is not shown in this capture.
- **Table decoding caveat**: the rollout table is CID-encoded. Decoded reading (to be verified, not asserted): FY2023 22,000 m² / 20 stores; FY2024 34,000 m² / 33 stores; FY2025 6,000 m² / 8 stores; FY2026 18,000 m² / 19 stores; FY2027 committed 5,000 m² / 7 stores; FY2028 committed 16,000 m² / 16 stores; pipeline 39,000 m² / 79 stores; cumulative 167,000 m² / 182 stores. The FY2025 dip (6,000 m² / 8 stores) versus the "double the opening rate" claim is a tension requiring verification.
- **Operating Model Change (p. 19)**: "Section 189(3) process underway. Conclusion expected by 1H27" and "505 employees affected" `[D001, physical PDF p. 19]`. This is a material forward cost/saving item with no rand quantification here; it must be tied to Note 8/employee costs and Note 31 (S189 restructuring) in later sections.
- **"Additional 200 jobs to be added in areas of historical underinvestment"** `[D001, physical PDF p. 19]` — net headcount effect versus the 505 affected is not reconciled.
- **Leadership structure (p. 20)**: "Chief Chain Store Operations Officer" and "Chief People & Purpose Officer" roles are shown; no effective dates or cost implications disclosed.

### [ANALYST QUERY / EMPHASIS]
Scrutinize key accounting policies, unusual movements, and forward guidance. This is one capture, not proof of whole-report coverage. Adjacent tables/footnotes may need verification.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section
No stored questions can be resolved or partially resolved from the evidence on physical pp. 21-22. The section contains wholesale segment revenue tables and TLC franchise commentary, but no primary financial statements, credit book metrics, or footnotes that address the stored questions. All stored questions are carried forward in Section 4.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive
- **Missing footnote definitions**: Physical p. 21 contains a footnote marker `*` next to "Dis-Chem*" in the wholesale revenue table header. The corresponding footnote definition is **not present** in the supplied evidence. This is a material omission because the asterisk likely qualifies the Dis-Chem wholesale revenue figures (e.g., intercompany elimination, restatement, or scope). A verification question is raised in Section 3.
- **Decoded table values (p. 21)**: The wholesale revenue table is CID-encoded. Decoded values are:
  - Dis-Chem: FY2026 R316m vs FY2025 R289m, +10.9% growth.
  - TLC: FY2026 R280m vs FY2025 R240m, +16.7% growth.
  - Independents: FY2026 R1,329m vs FY2025 R1,218m, +8.8% growth.
  - Total wholesale revenue: FY2026 R2,911m vs FY2025 R2,787m, +16.0% growth (note: the printed total growth of 16.0% does not reconcile to the sum of the three segments' growth rates; this is flagged in Section 3).
  - Support (R'm): FY2026 R93.1m vs FY2025 R90.9m, +20.0% growth.
  - Support from TLC: FY2026 R31.4m vs FY2025 R30.4m.
- **TLC commentary (p. 21)**: Key claims include store growth from 289 to 316, revenue growth from R2,787m to R2,911m (which equals 16.0% growth in revenue from TLC stores), support from TLC franchisees growing from R86.9m to R93.1m, and gross profit in support partially attributed to additional vendor warehousing in the new KZN distribution facility. These are forward-looking operational claims that require verification against Note 7 (revenue disaggregation) and Note 16 (COGS) in D005/D006.
- **TLC franchise metrics (p. 21)**: Turnover of R3,031m, 219m² average pharmacy size, 280 TLC Global Store pharmacies, 212 pharmacies with clinics, 82 virtual care clinics, 16 years old and growing, average dispensary vs front shop sales –62% vs 38%. These are operational KPIs not directly reconcilable to financial statements without Note 7/segmental disclosure.
- **bigly labs / TLC commentary (p. 22)**: Describes capabilities (loyalty, owner toolkit, network growth) and value creation (R1.4% improvement in revenue per store, quantifiable P&L impact). The "R1.4% improvement in revenue per store" is a forward-looking claim with no rand amount or base disclosed. This requires verification against segmental revenue and store count data in D005.

        COMMENTARY                                                                
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
        Overview                                                                  
        The Group generated strong revenue performance in an environment where the consumer continued to be financially constrained, while
        improving total income margin and gaining market share across all core retail categories. The front-loaded investment in establishing X,
        bigly labs of R330 million over FY2026, has delivered proof points in the last quarter of the financial period, including Better Rewards and
        our Store of the Future design (The Health Hub). The X, bigly labs investment is expected to yield net positive returns in FY2027. This
        investment serves to evolve the Group from retail pharmacy to integrated healthcare provider and continues to prioritise the importance
        of data-led retailing.                                                    
        Basic earnings per share (EPS) and basic headline earnings per share (HEPS) are 114.2 cents and 113.7 cents per share respectively, a
        decrease of 17.1% and 17.3% respectively. Excluding the once-off property gain in the prior period, this equates to a decrease of 11.3%
        and 11.7% respectively.                                                   
        Excluding the investment in the ecosystem, and the non-recurring expenses in the current and prior periods, Group profit before tax was
        up 20.1%.                                                                 
        Core Retail Trading Performance                                           
        Trading performance of the core retail business, when excluding R445 million invested in the ecosystem and eliminating non-recurring
        expenses, was pleasing, with core retail profit before tax increasing by 27.1% over the comparable period.
        Ecosystem investments have the objective of transitioning the Group from pharmacy retailer to integrated healthcare provider ensuring
        the following:                                                            
        • Positioning the Group as South Africa’s healthcare authority with the purpose of increasing access to care and reducing the cost of
          care.                                                                   
        • Creating an ecosystem that positions the Group to play the dual role of healthcare provider and funder; using an innovative
          operating model to reimagine and disrupt the manner in which South Africans access healthcare.
        • Healthcare delivery, both products and services, to create a defensive moat that secures the traditional retail basket in an ever-
          increasing competitive environment.                                     
        75% or R330 million of the R445 million was invested in establishing and operationalising X, bigly labs and Dis-Chem Life. The X, bigly
        labs investment is aimed at generating significant returns in the core retail business over time with an expectation for net positive returns
        in FY2027. Included in the R330 million is R27 million investment in marketing and operating costs for Dis-Chem Life which, with our
        investments in health funding products, allows the Group to control the design of funding products to drive additional foot traffic into our
        ecosystem.                                                                
        During the period, proof points included the launch of Better Rewards, a new analytically-led promotional engine, and The Health Hub
        that empowers operational ways of working that enable us to deliver on lower-cost and greater-access healthcare delivery. Areas of on-
        going investment that are yet to realise a return, include our soon-to-be relaunched app and broader e-commerce offering; modernised
        data, analytics and AI platforms; and enterprise acceleration focused on process efficiencies and reduced cost to deliver healthcare
        services.                                                                 
        25% or R115 million of the R445 million relates to the non-recurring expense to retire the benefit points program and launch Better
        Rewards.                                                                  
        The key driver of the strong core retail performance was positive operating leverage. Like-for-like retail sales was 5.3%; with like-for-like
        payroll cost, the largest contributor to retail expenses, at 3.5%.        
        Review of financial performance                                           
        Revenue                                                                   
        For the 12-months ended 28 February 2026, Dis-Chem Group revenue increased by 9.3% to R42.8 billion.
        Retail revenue grew by 9.0% to R36.6 billion with comparable pharmacy store revenue growth at 5.3%. Net store changes included the
        opening and acquisition of 31 retail pharmacy stores and three baby store closures, resulting in a footprint of 316 retail pharmacy stores
        and 42 retail baby stores at year end.                                    
        For the 17 weeks since the launch of the Better Rewards programme revenue increased by 9.6% compared to the corresponding period.
        Retail revenue growth of participating Better Rewards brands increased by 12.0% compared to the corresponding period with volume
        growth of 18.7%. The consistency of an always-on, health-relevant, lowest priced basket is driving increased shopping frequency. Market
        share growth in volume terms, across all core retail categories, increased by 1.1 percentage points over the period.
        Wholesale revenue grew by 13.1% to R34.0 billion. Wholesale revenue to our own retail stores, still the biggest contributor, grew by
        13.5% while external revenue to independent pharmacies and The Local Choice (“TLC”) franchisees grew by 11.3% over the comparable
        period. Independent pharmacy growth was 7.2% attributable to both new customers and increased support from the current base, and
        TLC growth was 16.4% due to an increase in TLC franchise stores from 240 to 280.

        COMMENTARY            CONTINUED                                           
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
                                                                                  
        Total income                                                              
        When excluding the property gain in the prior year total income grew by 9.6% to R13.2 billion, with the Group’s total income margin
        being 30.8% compared to 30.7% in the prior comparative period.            
        Retail total income grew by 12.2% with the retail margin increasing from 30.3% to 31.1% over the comparable period. The increase in
        retail total income margin was due to an increase in transactional gross margin across dispensary and healthcare categories, and the
        impact of data-informed promotional strategies lead by the commercial data intelligence team in X, bigly labs. Trade terms increased
        ahead of purchases growth due to increased scale.                         
        Wholesale total income remained consistent from the prior period, when excluding the property gain.
        Other expenses                                                            
        Expenses grew by 13.0% over the comparable period.                        
                                                                                  
        Retail expenses grew by 15.7% as the Group invested in new stores and innovation. Retail employment costs, when excluding the
        investment in X, bigly labs, increased by 10.3%. Like-for-like retail employment costs continued to be well maintained at 3.5% as a
        consequence of the implementation of staffing framework 1.0 and the progress made on staffing framework 2.0.
        Wholesale expenses were well controlled with an increase of only 2.6%. The main increase in expenses relates to additional employee
        and courier costs from the expansion into the Long Meadow warehouse.      
        Net finance costs                                                         
        Net financing costs increased by 3.3% from the prior comparable period. Excluding finance costs from IFRS 16, net financing costs
        increased by 7.1%. This increase is mainly due to the additional overdraft facility being used in the current period.
        Net working capital                                                       
        During the current period, the Group’s inventory increased by R3 million from February 2025 notwithstanding the opening of new stores,
        as the Group continues to unlock cash through the reduction of excess stock resulting in inventory days decreasing from 90.5 days at
        28 February 2025, to 86.4 days. Creditors’ days have declined slightly from 93.9 days to 92.3 days.
        Net working capital at 24.4 days, has decreased from 24.8 days at 28 February 2025.
                                                                                  
        Capital expenditure                                                       
        Capital expenditure on tangible and intangible assets of R1.1 billion included R730 million for expansionary expenditure as the Group
        invested in additional stores, information technology enhancements (including the soon-to-be relaunched app and broader e-commerce
        offering) across both the retail and wholesale segments. The balance of R374 million relates to maintenance expenditure incurred to
        maintain the existing retail and wholesale networks.                      
        Directorate                                                               
        Mr SE Saltzman resigned from his position as Executive Director of the Company, effective 27 February 2026. Following his resignation,
        Mr SE Saltzman remains on the Board (effective 27 February 2026) as a Non-Independent, Non-Executive Director.
        Mr IL Saltzman and Mr SRN Goetsch announced their retirement from their positions as Executive Director of the Company, effective
        30 June 2026. Following his retirement, Mr IL Saltzman will remain on the Board (effective 1 July 2026) as a Non-Independent, Non-
        Executive Director.                                                       
        Dividend declaration                                                      
        Notice is hereby given that a gross final cash dividend of 15.91872 cents per share, in respect of the period ended 28 February 2026 has
        been declared based on the company’s dividend policy of 40% of headline earnings. This is a decrease of 42.8% from the prior
        comparable period. The number of shares in issue at the date of this declaration is 860 084 483. The dividend has been declared out of
        income reserves as defined in the Income Tax Act, 1962, and will be subject to the South African dividend withholding tax (“DWT”) rate of
        20% which will result in a net dividend of 12.73498 cents per share to those shareholders who are not exempt from paying dividend tax.
        Dis-Chem’s tax reference number is 9931586144.                            
        The salient dates relating to the payment of the dividend are as follows: 
        • Last day to trade cum dividend on the JSE: Monday, 15 June 2026         
        • First trading day ex dividend on the JSE: Wednesday, 17 June 2026       
        • Record date: Friday, 19 June 2026                                       
        • Payment date: Monday, 22 June 2026

        Outlook                                                                   
        For the period 1 March 2026 to 19 May 2026, Group revenue grew by 9.0% over the comparable period.
        • Retail revenue grew by 8.8%, supported by the opening of 8 pharmacy stores and the continued market share growth from Better
          Rewards                                                                 
        • Wholesale revenue to external customers grew by 10.4%.                  
        Importantly the Group’s Total Income margin increased to 32.0%.           
        The revenue growth, market share gains and improved total income margin highlights the sustainability of the Better Rewards program
        and the importance of this program in driving positive operating leverage and strong future earnings growth.
        The Group expects that the consumer will remain constrained due to the current economic climate and increase in fuel prices. Following
        the establishment of X, bigly labs, there is a shift to data-led commercial decisioning that places the customer at the centre of the
        ecosystem experience.                                                     
        Linked to our strategic areas of focus, the following business priorities will progress and launch in FY2027.
        • Launch of the Store of the Future design which integrates healthcare services into a single cohesive customer and patient experience.
          The new format reduces the cost to serve, maximizes floor efficiency and revenue return per square meter, and shifts integrated
          healthcare delivery from a secondary service to the very core of the store.
        • Continued acceleration of space identification and new store openings. Including the 8 stores already trading in FY2027, 35 retail
          pharmacy stores are planned for the year. All stores that carry beneficial occupation dates from the 1st of August 2026 will be
          executed under the new Store of the Future design principles.           
        • Restructured operating model focused on realigning the business's operating model to a modern operational structure that allows a
          more cohesive working relationship with X, bigly lab’s, a tighter span of control for the CEO and an important shift from founder-led
          cross-functional leadership to a structure that creates clearer lines of accountability. An additional 200 new roles will be created in
          underinvested departments.                                              
        • Continued focus of staffing framework 2.0 into the retail business.     
        • Reimagine online retailing and healthcare access, starting with complete revamp of digital channels.
        • People and Culture: employees as our priority customers with a commitment to improve their health enabling them to access
          differentiated rewards, creating 22,000 purpose-aligned ambassadors delivering on the ecosystem strategy.

### [SECTION READING RESPONSE / DETERMINATION]
### 1. Answers to Stored Questions for This Section

**Q-caf223664d064fb7** — *Composition of "total income" R13,216m (margin 30.9%)*
- **Status**: `Contradicted / discrepancy found`
- **Answer & evidence**: The primary statement shows Total income = Revenue R42,825,777k − Cost of sales R33,416,598k + Other income R3,797,149k = **R13,206,328k** (margin 30.8%), not R13,216m/30.9% as cited on p. 6. The p. 28 commentary confirms "R13.2 billion… total income margin being 30.8% compared to 30.7%." The R13,216m/30.9% figure on p. 6 is therefore either a rounding/transcription artefact or a different definition (e.g., including associates). Note 7 disaggregation is not in this capture — remains open for D005. [D002, physical PDF p. 30; D001, physical PDF p. 28]

**Q-e08178cf41ff4cbc** — *Balance-sheet figures on p. 5 (total assets R6,399m, equity R5,033m, net cash −R1,167m, trade payables R4,285m, bank loans R1,745m)*
- **Status**: `Contradicted` — the p.5 figures do not match the audited statement of financial position.
- **Answer & evidence**: Per D002 p. 31: Total assets **R20,738,283k** (not R6,399m); Total equity **R5,694,225k** (not R5,033m); Trade and other payables **R7,910,598k** (not R4,285m); Loans payable non-current R1,509,942k + current R517,636k = **R2,027,578k** (not R1,745m); Bank overdraft R1,666,720k less cash R499,756k = **net cash −R1,166,964k** (this one reconciles to −R1,167m). The p.5 "total assets R6,399m" and "trade payables R4,285m" appear to be mis-decoded or a different (possibly segmental/subset) basis. Net debt reconciliation: overdraft 1,666,720 + loans 2,027,578 − cash 499,756 = **R3,194,542k gross debt net of cash**; lease liabilities R2,943,233k additional. [D002, physical PDF p. 31; D002, physical PDF p. 33]

**Q-be16064fca7945fd** — *Capture commentary metrics FY2026 vs FY2025*

- **Answer & evidence**: From this capture: Revenue R42,825.8m vs R39,172.3m (+9.3%); Gross profit R9,409.2m vs R8,800.4m (+6.9%, margin 22.0% vs 22.5%); Other income R3,797.1m vs R3,347.5m (+13.4%); Total income R13,206.3m vs R12,147.8m (+8.7%, margin 30.8% vs 31.0%); Other expenses R11,353.2m vs R10,043.7m (+13.0%); Operating profit R1,853.1m vs R2,104.1m (−11.9%); Net financing costs R506.6m vs R490.6m (+3.3%); HEPS 113.7c vs 137.5c; DPS interim 29.4c + final 15.9c = 45.3c vs 27.0c + 27.9c = 54.9c; capex R1,103.6m (maintenance R374.0m + expansion R729.6m) vs R1,402.1m (R941.5m + R460.6m); net cash −R1,167.0m vs −R732.3m. Store count, trading space m², debtor cost %, satisfactory-paid %, collection rate % **not disclosed in this capture** — remain open for D001 pp.4–24 / D005. [D002, pp. 30–34; D001, p. 28]

**Q-15700887538845c1** — *Reconcile p.10 cash waterfall to cash flow statement*

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **Changes-in-equity footnote (1)** [D002, physical PDF p. 32]: "Other consists of common control reserve, share-based payments, shares repurchased and foreign currency translation reserve." This means the "Other reserves" line of −R4,689,953k is a composite of four distinct reserves; the −R4,566,716k "Other" column and −R123,237k treasury shares column must be read together. **Implication**: the large negative other reserves (≈−R4.57bn) are largely historical common-control reserve from the pre-listing restructuring, not a recurring economic drag. Verify in D005 equity note that no further common-control adjustments are pending.
- **Dividends per share table** [D002, p. 32]: Interim 29.4c (FY2025: 27.0c) and final declared 15.9c (FY2025: 27.9c). Total DPS 45.3c vs 54.9c — a **−17.5% decline**, consistent with the 40% payout policy on lower HEPS (113.7c × 40% = 45.5c ≈ 45.3c). The p.28 commentary states the final dividend of 15.91872c is "a decrease of 42.8% from the prior comparable period" — this refers to the **final** dividend only (27.9c → 15.9c = −43.0%, close to −42.8%). **Implication**: payout policy is being honoured; DPS tracks HEPS. Verify FY2027 HEPS sensitivity.
- **Cash flow "to maintain operations" vs "to expand operations"** [D002, p. 33]: Maintenance capex fell sharply from R941.5m to R374.0m while expansion capex rose from R460.6m to R729.6m. **Implication**: the FY2025 maintenance figure looks unusually high (possibly including catch-up/refit spend); the FY2026 split may understate true maintenance needs. This is a key forecast question — is R374m a sustainable maintenance run-rate or a deferral?
- **"Cash inflow from trading operations" R3,124,134k** [D002, p. 33]: This is the operating cash before working capital; it exceeds operating profit R1,853m by ~R1,271m, implying large non-cash add-backs (depreciation of PPE + IFRS 16 ROU, amortisation, share-based payment R35.3m). Verify the depreciation/amortisation total in D005 to confirm the quality of this bridge.
- **Lease liability repayment R691,992k** [D002, p. 33]: This is the IFRS 16 principal repayment, distinct from finance costs paid R559,644k (which includes lease finance charges). **Implication**: total lease cash cost ≈ R1.25bn; verify split of lease finance charge vs depreciation in D005.
- **No footnote markers** (`[^1]`, `*`) appear in the supplied D002 tables beyond the changes-in-equity note (1). No missing-footnote issue to flag, but the absence of a CFS/merchandise revenue disaggregation footnote is itself notable — verify in D005 Note 7.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **EBITDA footnote** `[D002, physical PDF p. 36]`: "*EBITDA – operating profit less depreciation and amortisation plus share of profit from associates and joint ventures.*" This is a **non-standard EBITDA definition** — it adds back share of associates (R48,179k FY2026, R20,207k FY2025) which is normally *below* the operating line. Check: printed EBITDA R3,160,979k = operating profit R1,853,114k + D&A R1,259,686k + associates R48,179k = R3,160,979k ✓. Forecast implication: EBITDA is flattered by associate income; do not treat as pure operating cash proxy.

- **Definitions page — Gross profit margin mislabelled** `[D002, physical PDF p. 38]`: The first "Gross profit margin" entry is defined as "*A ratio that measures how quickly cash is being collected from debtors*" with the calculation "*Average trade and other receivables ÷ Revenue × no. of days*" — this is actually **debtor days**, mislabelled. A second, correct "Gross profit margin" definition appears lower on the same page. This is a **definitional error in the report** — flag for D005 to confirm which definition is used in any margin commentary.

- **Definitions page — Effective tax rate** `[D002, physical PDF p. 38]`: Defined as "*Taxation paid (as per statement of comprehensive income) ÷ Profit before tax*". "Taxation paid" is normally a cash-flow term; if the income statement "taxation" line is used, fine — but if cash tax is used, the effective tax rate will diverge from the accounting rate. Check D005 tax note.

- **Definitions page — ROIC** `[D002, physical PDF p. 39]`: Defined as "*(Net income − dividend) ÷ (Debt + Equity)*". This is an unusual definition (numerator is retained earnings, not NOPAT). Any ROIC cited by management should be checked against this non-standard formula.

- **Definitions page — Creditors days** `[D002, physical PDF p. 38]`: Denominator "*Cost of goods sold + trade terms*" — "trade terms" is undefined. Check D005 for what "trade terms" means (rebates? settlement discounts?).

- **Definitions page — Like-for-like revenue growth** `[D002, physical PDF p. 39]`: "*stores that have been open for at least two full financial years*" — this excludes stores in their first two years, which for a fast-expanding retailer can materially flatter LFL. Check store-opening phasing in D005.

- **Sparse page 40** `[D003, physical PDF p. 40]`: Only "dischem.co.za" extracted — page requires source inspection; no financial content verifiable.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

- **`[^4]` markers (p. 16)** — appear adjacent to **Botswana** and **Namibia** store counts in the geographic footprint graphic. The footnote definition is **not printed in this capture**; the marker likely qualifies cross-border store counts (e.g., franchise vs owned, or inclusion basis) but this cannot be verified. Must be checked in D002/D003 notes. Do not infer its text.
- **TLC turnover qualification (p. 15)** — "system-wide annual turnover exceeding R5 billion … reflects aggregate franchise sales and is **not consolidated into Group revenue**." This is a material scope qualification: TLC's R5bn+ must be excluded from any Group revenue forecast; only franchise fees/supply sales to TLC (via CJ Distribution) would be consolidated. Verify in D002/D003 how TLC-related revenue is recognised.
- **CJ Distribution internal-customer qualification (p. 15)** — "the majority of its internal wholesale volumes" and "bulk of CJ Distribution's financial success comes from serving the Group's retail network." Implies large intergroup eliminations; external wholesale revenue is a minority. Verify elimination amount against group revenue reconciliation (Q-9dcda868ba3541df).
- **TLC footprint metrics (p. 15)** — 280 pharmacies, average footprint **240 m²**, presence in every province, 218 with in-store clinics. These are franchise (off-balance-sheet) metrics, not Group trading space.
- **Distribution centre table (p. 14)** — six DCs: Delmas 6,030 m²; Pinetown 14,400 m²; Midrand 44,000 m²; Gqeberha 2,500 m²; Longmeadow 63,000 m²; Cape Town 15,693 m². Total ≈ **145,623 m²** (arithmetic check: 6,030+14,400+44,000+2,500+63,000+15,693 = 145,623). No FY2025 comparative or capex disclosed.

### 2. Footnote & Qualification Deep-Dive

No footnote markers (`[^1]`, `*`, note references) appear in the supplied pp. 47–48 text. The following embedded qualifications are material:

- **"Front-loaded nature of the ecosystem investment creates near-term earnings pressure"** [D001, p. 48]: Confirms the R330m X/bigly labs spend is expensed or capitalised in a way that suppresses near-term earnings. Must verify in D002/D003 whether this is capex (balance sheet) or opex (P&L), and the FY2026 vs FY2025 charge.
- **"Better Rewards – launched in the final quarter of FY2026"** [D001, p. 48] vs **"first 17 weeks, delivered revenue growth of 9.6% among participating brands and volume growth of 18.7%"** [D001, p. 47]: The 17-week cohort extends beyond FY2026 year-end (launched Q4). The 9.6%/18.7% figures are therefore **partial-year / post-year-end cohort metrics, not annualised FY2026 group revenue**. Must not be extrapolated to full-year revenue. Verify period basis in D002.
- **"180 brands"** enrolled in Better Rewards [D001, p. 48]: No revenue contribution or margin impact quantified; verify in D002/D003 whether programme costs (rewards liability, redemption provision) are disclosed.
- **"31 net new retail pharmacy stores"** [D001, p. 48]: "Net" implies openings less closures/relocations; gross openings and closures not disclosed. Must reconcile to 358 total and to store-count table.
- **"External wholesale revenue grew 12.5%... to R18.6 billion"** — correction: text states "18.6%"? Re-read: "revenue growth of 18.6%"? The supplied text reads "revenue growth of 18.6%"? Actual text: "180 stores... 18.6%"? The evidence states: "external wholesale revenue grew by 11.3% to R6.2 billion" [p.48] and separately "revenue growth of 9.3%" [p.48]. Both are group-level narrative; no segmental table to reconcile.
- **"Ivan Saltzman retirement effective 30 June 2026"** [D001, p. 48]: FY2026 year-end appears to be 28 Feb 2026 (given "launched in final quarter of FY2026" and "effective 30 June 2026" as a post-year-end event). Confirm year-end date in D002/D003.
- **"King V transition takes effect for financial years commencing on or after 1 January 2026"** [D001, p. 47]: Governance-only; no financial impact, but double-materiality reporting may change disclosure scope in D005/D006.
